pages.title: Welcome to Personal branding for career success

blocks.text: Welcome to this free course, *Personal branding for career success*. The course lasts eight weeks, with approximately three hours of study each week. You can work at your own pace, so if you have more time one week there is no problem with pushing on to complete another week's study.
You can test your understanding through the weekly quizzes; in the original course, the Week 4 and Week 8 quizzes give you the opportunity to earn a badge.
After completing this course, you will be able to:

items: describe what personal branding is and understand how the concept can help you in your career
understand how relevant marketing techniques and tactics can be applied to branding a person
define your own, authentic personal brand and know who you want to market it to and why
promote yourself effectively to employers, both in your workplace and beyond
devise an appropriate plan of action to develop and promote your personal brand and enhance your career

blocks.text: Each week ends with a summary that leads you on to the next week, and you can return to the course contents at any time to move to any part of the course.

The course is not intended to be an academic course but a self-help career guide to personal branding. You will see references both to academic research and to online blog content, because many experienced individuals share their commentary in popular books and online rather than in academic publications.

blocks.title: Plan your study
blocks.text: To complete the course you need about 24 hours of study time over about 8 weeks, but you can study at any time and at a pace to suit you.
The Open University also invites learners to complete an optional, confidential start-of-course survey about themselves and their expectations.

While studying this course you have the option to work towards a digital badge. Badged courses are a key part of The Open University's mission *to promote the educational well-being of the community*, and help you progress from informal to formal learning. They are free and differ from formal courses because there is no tutor support, but you do get useful feedback from the interactive quizzes.

Digital badges are a way of demonstrating online that you have gained a skill. They help learners gain recognition and help employers identify the right candidate. You can share them with friends, family, employers and on social media; they are a great motivation and often boost confidence.

blocks.caption: The Personal Branding badge

blocks.text: What you have to do

items: read each week of the course
score 50% or more in the two badge quizzes in Week 4 and Week 8

blocks.text: For all the quizzes you can have up to three attempts at most questions (true/false questions usually allow one attempt). A correct answer first time earns more marks than one on the second or third attempt, so it is possible to get every question right and still not reach 50%. Wrong answers often come with helpful feedback.

If you don't reach 50% in a badge quiz, you can retry the whole quiz after 24 hours, as many times as you like. See getting a badge as an opportunity to reflect on what you have learned rather than as a test.

pages.title: Week 1: Where am I starting from?

blocks.text: Welcome to Week 1. Congratulations! You are on your way to developing a new personal brand that will enhance your professional profile and your career. Whether you are starting from scratch or looking to enhance an existing brand, this course can help you.

blocks.title: Video 1 Introduction to Week 1 (no spoken audio)
blocks.note: Animated text introducing the week: you start by asking 'what is a personal brand?', see definitions from academics and business professionals, explore the pros and cons of developing a personal brand, think about how you might describe yourself to a stranger, identify your aims for the course and use time management tools to find time to study.

blocks.text: By the end of this week, you will be able to:

items: recognise what a personal brand is
review your current personal brand
identify areas of interest based on your current aims and aspirations

blocks.text: We all have a brand already. It reflects our values, beliefs and personal qualities and determines how they come across to other people. As Jeff Bezos, CEO of Amazon, famously said:
Your brand is what people say about you when you're not in the room.

blocks.alt: A bearded man wearing glasses holds up a Post-it note reading 'You are your own brand'
blocks.caption: Figure 1 You are your own brand

blocks.text: McNally and Speak (2009, p.4) start from a well-defined concept of a brand: '...a perception or emotion, maintained by a buyer or a prospective buyer, describing the experience related to doing business with an organisation or consuming its products or services.'

blocks.title: Personal brand (McNally and Speak, 2009)
blocks.text: 'Your brand is a perception or emotion, maintained by somebody other than you, that describes the total experience of having a relationship with you.'

Your brand is a reflection of who you are and what you believe, which is visibly expressed by what you do and how you do it. It's the doing part that connects you with someone else, and that connection with someone else results in a relationship.

Personal branding is viewed by academics and professionals in many different ways, and not always positively. For some, defining and understanding your personal brand is an obvious path to living a better life:
Building an authentic personal brand is an evolutionary and organic process and a journey towards a successful life.
For Tom Peters, widely quoted as the first to talk about the concept, it is the only way to develop and progress in your career:

Regardless of age, regardless of position, regardless of the business we happen to be in, all of us need to understand the importance of branding. We are CEOs of our own companies: Me Inc. To be in business today, our most important job is to be a head marketer for the brand called You.

pages.title: Celebrity, cynicism and this course's view

blocks.text: Many of us associate personal branding with entrepreneurship, or even celebrity, when individuals become the face of their own brand:
A great way to understand the concept is as follows... when somebody hears your name, what pops into their head? That's your brand, for better or for worse.
For some it represents a cynicism that has affected many of our lives, for example through the rise of reality TV:

The branded self is one of the more cynical products of the era of the flexible personality: a form of self-presentation singularly focused on attracting attention and acquiring cultural and monetary value.

blocks.title: This course's approach
blocks.text: Personal branding is treated as a useful tool for promoting yourself effectively and consistently to employers, current and future, helping you gain greater job satisfaction and progress your career as you want to.
Allow about 5 minutes.

blocks.title: Video 2 Different ideas about personal brand
blocks.note: A short video of different quotes, definitions and opinions about what a personal brand is.

blocks.title: Activity 1 Quotes, definitions and opinions
blocks.prompt: Watch the video and make a note of any quotes that particularly catch your eye or seem to encapsulate your own perception of what personal branding is.
blocks.model: What stood out may have been the focus on being yourself, using your talent or making a strong impression on others. Although there are many definitions available, your personal brand is just that - 'personal'. In fact, it is unique to you, and you'll explore this in more detail as you work through the course.
points: Names a quote or idea that stood out and why
Links it to being yourself, using your talent or making an impression on others
Recognises that a personal brand is personal and unique to you

blocks.text: What are some of the potential pros and cons for you when developing your personal brand? First, the positives.

items: *Helps you to stand out.* A strong brand lets you communicate clearly to recruiters or customers. If they can easily see that your skills and values align with what they are looking for, they are more likely to engage with you.
*Networking becomes easier.* A clear brand helps you a) identify the people you want to network with and b) have concise, effective points to make in conversation (more in Week 7).

*Supports career decision making.* An authentic brand involves considering what you want from your career and what you have to offer, which makes choosing which job to apply for or which offer to accept easier.

blocks.alt: A person holds a green circle with a plus sign in one hand and a red circle with a minus sign in the other
blocks.caption: Figure 2 There are always pros and cons

items: *Lack of authenticity.* For many, authenticity is an important element of a successful brand. Presenting a brand that doesn't honestly represent who you are, day after day, to employers, colleagues and peers, will be hard work and often personally unfulfilling.

*Too much self disclosure.* Personal branding involves self-disclosure. How far you embrace that is up to you; there may be a line you are not prepared to cross, e.g. sharing your opinions openly on social media (more in Week 6).

*Time consuming.* Developing and promoting your brand - contacting the right people, putting relevant commentary on social media, etc. - takes time, so you must be prepared to commit to doing it properly.

blocks.q: Which of these is described as a potential pitfall of personal branding?
options: Presenting a brand that doesn't honestly represent who you are
It makes career decisions more difficult
blocks.explain: Lack of authenticity is a pitfall; easier networking and support for career decisions are listed as positives.

blocks.text: Not everyone supports personal branding. Sheryl Sandberg, Chief Operating Officer of Facebook, was asked how business people should manage their personal brands:

You don't have a brand. I get this question a lot, and I shudder every time. Crest has a brand. Perrier has a brand. People are not that simple. When we are packaged, we're ineffective and inauthentic.
Her advice is 'Don't package yourself. Just speak honestly, factually and from your own experience'.

Sandberg makes a useful point about the potential to take personal branding too far; in Week 2 you'll look at what we can learn from branding a product. Even if you are uncomfortable with a whole branding exercise, some components of the process, e.g. developing your LinkedIn profile effectively, can be useful for anyone.
Allow about 10 minutes.

blocks.title: Activity 2 Having a strong brand
blocks.prompt: Consider someone you think has a strong personal brand - someone you know (at work, in your social circle) or someone in the media. With Jeff Bezos' quote in mind, what do people say about them when they aren't in the room? List the words that spring to mind. Then note how that person communicates their brand: e.g. are they always positive in meetings, do they volunteer for unpopular tasks, talk about what they stand for, contribute consistently? Do you think their brand has had a positive impact on their career?
blocks.model: You might have chosen words like 'consistent', 'interesting', 'attention-seeking', 'friendly' or 'authoritative'. They might not all be things you'd want said about you, but they show that person's impact on those around them. A celebrity such as Angelina Jolie, an ambassador for the UN Refugee Agency, has a hugely effective brand with millions of followers: you may not share what she stands for, but her brand is clear and has helped develop her career and causes.
points: Lists words people use about the person when they are not in the room
Describes how the person communicates their brand through behaviour
Judges whether the brand has had a positive impact on their career
Recognises that a brand reflects a person's impact on those around them

blocks.text: Take a moment to consider the personal brand that you currently have. This will give you a starting point to build from as you work through the course.

blocks.alt: A smiling woman wearing glasses holds up an empty business card
blocks.caption: Figure 3 What's your personal brand?

blocks.title: Activity 3 Describing my brand to a stranger
blocks.prompt: Allow about 30 minutes. How would you describe yourself to a stranger in three workplace-relevant words? Some to get you started: honest, creative, diligent, trustworthy, positive, innovative, organised, empathetic, effective, accurate, detailed, questioning, friendly, problem solver, supportive, dedicated, reliable, ambitious, flexible, thorough, focused. Then ask three people you trust (colleagues, friends, family) for three words each and add them. Were they similar to yours, or were there surprises? Do you like how they described you, or would you like to change their perception?
blocks.model: Understanding how others perceive you, and how that compares with your own view, is a useful starting point. From there you can decide whether your current brand aligns with how you want to be seen, and whether it will help your career plans - or whether you need to change the brand or the plans. Something you see as positive may be seen as negative: 'creative and innovative' may not suit a role that follows established procedures, and 'thorough' might look 'obsessive' to someone else.
points: Gives three self-description words and words from three other people
Compares own view with how others see them
Considers whether this brand supports current career plans
Notes that a trait seen as positive may be seen as negative by others

blocks.text: Because personal branding can be applied in so many ways, be clear about why you want to develop yours at this point in your career. For example, you might be looking for:

items: a clearer sense of who you are and what you have to offer - increasing your clarity and confidence
a chance to rebrand - if your priorities have changed and your brand no longer reflects what you want from your career
further development in your workplace - maximising the chances of your name coming up when opportunities or vacancies arise
a clear, consistent message for your networks, off and online - making networking easier and leading to interesting connections
ideas to promote yourself to new employers, e.g. through applications and interviews - which can make a significant difference to your success rate

blocks.alt: A hand holds a camera lens in front of blurred woodland; through the lens the trees are sharp
blocks.caption: Figure 4 Be clear

pages.title: Activity 4 What do I want my personal brand to do for my career?

blocks.text: Allow about 10 minutes.

blocks.title: Activity 4 What do I want my personal brand to do for my career?
blocks.prompt: Explain why you want to develop your personal brand. Which of the aims (clarity about yourself, a rebrand, development at work, a consistent message for your networks, promoting yourself to new employers) apply to you?
blocks.model: Knowing why you want to develop your personal brand and how you want to use it will help to inform your progress through the course. Whatever stage you are at, the course is designed to share something useful each week, but some weeks may be more relevant to your journey than others.
points: States a clear reason for developing a personal brand
Links the reason to a specific aim such as rebranding, promotion or finding a new employer
Considers how the brand will be used in their career

pages.title: Ten benefits of a personal brand

blocks.text: Executive Career Coach Susan Chritton's blog (n.d.) lists ten benefits:

items: **Permission to be yourself** - express your authentic self
**Gains in confidence** - know you have something of value to offer
**Building credibility** - through consistent actions that align with your brand
**Showcasing your specialty** - your unique mix of work experience, life experience and personal characteristics determines your niche
**Leaving your mark** - people remember your actions, expertise and emotional connections
**Connection to your target audience** - clear, consistent interaction that quickly becomes familiar
**Distinguishing yourself from the competition** - your target market discerns something different about you
**The support you need** - be clear about what you need so you can ask with clarity
**Focusing your energy** - use your brand as a filter to decide what to focus on
**Letting yourself be lazy** - a brand thrives on consistency, so once it's right you don't need to re-invent yourself

blocks.text: We all experience time pressure, and the first things we drop are often activities we take on for our own development or enjoyment. Spending a little time identifying when you can work on the course each week, and deliberately setting that time aside, can make a difference.

Allow a minimum of three hours each week. If possible, choose times when you can bring energy and attention to the task: if you function better in the mornings, set your alarm earlier and complete a section before your daily routine; if you are more energetic in the evening, allocate time towards the end of each day.

blocks.alt: A hand holds a black alarm clock surrounded by colourful drawings of things that take up time, such as books, a laptop, a coffee cup and a paper aeroplane
blocks.caption: Figure 5 Fitting it in

pages.title: Activity 5 How do I spend my time?

blocks.text: Allow about 15 minutes. The original activity provides a schedule (Table 1 Hours spent) of 90-minute blocks between 8 am and 11 pm for each day of the week: 08:00-09:30, 09:30-11:00, 11:00-12:30, 12:30-14:00, 14:00-15:30, 15:30-17:00, 17:00-18:30, 18:30-20:00, 20:00-21:30 and 21:30-23:00. It assumes most people sleep between 11 pm and 8 am, but adapt it to your own circumstances.

blocks.title: Activity 5 How do I spend my time?
blocks.prompt: Using the 90-minute blocks from Monday to Sunday, note how you spend the hours in each block. Then identify which blocks you could set aside for this course (at least three hours a week) and when you have most energy.
blocks.hint: Write it day by day, e.g. 'Mon 08:00-09:30 commute; 20:00-21:30 free'.
blocks.model: After completing the schedule you should have a clearer idea of the time available in your usual week and be able to identify blocks you could devote to the course and to any goals you set yourself. If you need more help, a time management tool can help you break large tasks down and be realistic about your priorities.
points: Describes how time is currently spent across the week
Identifies specific blocks of time for studying the course
Allows at least three hours per week
Chooses times when energy and attention are high

blocks.text: Now that you've completed Week 1, take this short quiz to reflect on what you've learned.

blocks.q: According to Jeff Bezos, what is your brand?
options: The logo and colours you use online
What people say about you when you're not in the room
The job title on your CV
blocks.explain: Bezos famously said 'Your brand is what people say about you when you're not in the room.'

blocks.q: In McNally and Speak's definition, who maintains the perception or emotion that makes up your personal brand?
blocks.explain: Your brand is 'a perception or emotion, maintained by somebody other than you, that describes the total experience of having a relationship with you.'

blocks.q: Who is widely quoted as the first person to talk about the concept of a personal brand, describing 'the brand called You'?
blocks.explain: Tom Peters (1997) said we are CEOs of our own companies, 'Me Inc.', and heads of marketing for 'the brand called You'.

blocks.q: Which of these are listed as positives of developing a personal brand? Select all that apply.
options: It helps you to stand out
blocks.explain: Standing out, easier networking and support for career decisions are the positives; branding is actually time consuming, which is listed as a pitfall.

blocks.q: Sheryl Sandberg advises business people to package themselves carefully as a brand, just like Crest or Perrier.
blocks.explain: Sandberg said 'You don't have a brand... People are not that simple' and advised 'Don't package yourself. Just speak honestly, factually and from your own experience'.

blocks.q: A characteristic you see as positive, such as being 'thorough', might be perceived negatively by someone else.
blocks.explain: Someone might see 'thorough' as 'obsessive', or 'creative and innovative' as unsuited to a role that follows established procedures.

blocks.text: By this point you should have a better understanding of what personal branding is all about. You've considered how different authors view it and some of the advantages you can gain from it. You've also reflected on your own personal brand and why you want to develop it.
You should now be able to:

items: recognise what a personal brand is
review your current personal brand
identify areas of interest based on your current aims and aspirations

cards.back: A perception or emotion, maintained by somebody other than you, that describes the total experience of having a relationship with you (McNally and Speak, 2009).
Tom Peters' idea that we are CEOs of our own companies and head marketers for 'the brand called You'.
Presenting a brand that honestly represents who you are; a brand that doesn't is hard work and often unfulfilling.
Sharing information and opinions about yourself; how far you go is your choice.

blocks.text: Next week, you'll focus on what makes a successful brand.

chapters.title: Week 2: Understanding marketing principles and practices
chapters.summary: What marketers know about successful brands - values, vision, personality, target audience, positioning and consistency - and how it applies to you.

pages.title: Week 2: Understanding marketing principles and practices

blocks.text: Last week you were introduced to personal branding, considering your own brand and why you want to develop it. This week you'll pause to look at approaches used by marketing teams when branding organisations and products. This is a much more familiar area of branding for most of us, and understanding the key elements of a good brand here gives useful insight into how to develop and promote your own.

blocks.title: Video 1 Introduction to Week 2 (no spoken audio)
blocks.note: Animated text: this week focuses on what can be learned from the way marketing professionals brand products and organisations - their tactics and techniques, the key elements of a successful brand, the concept of a target audience and the importance of brand positioning - and how these principles can boost your own personal brand.

blocks.text: By the end of this week, you will be able to:

items: describe the key elements of a successful brand
appreciate the concept of target audience
recognise the importance of positioning a brand correctly

blocks.text: The Design Council's *Power of Branding* (n.d.) describes 'four cornerstones' of any good brand:

items: **The big idea** - what lies at the heart of your company?
**Values** - what do you believe in?
**Vision** - where are you going?
**Personality** - how do you want to come across?

blocks.text: These cornerstones apply equally to personal branding. The Design Council suggests relevant questions to ask yourself: What is your offer? What makes you different? What is your 'personality'? What do consumers want or need?

blocks.alt: Illuminated digital advertising signs for well-known brands at Piccadilly Circus, London, at night
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Successful brands

blocks.text: Author and motivational speaker Simon Sinek is very clear about what makes one brand more successful than another.

blocks.title: Video 2 Simon Sinek - Start With Why - TED Talk
blocks.note: A short excerpt from Sinek's 2009 TED Talk 'How Great Leaders Inspire Action'. He explains his Golden Circle model: successful organisations communicate *why* they do what they do, not just what they do. The full talk goes on to explain why the human brain responds so well to starting with 'why'.

blocks.title: The Golden Circle
blocks.text: Sinek's model focuses on *why* a particular organisation does what it does, and *why* presenting this clearly to customers can lead to greater success.

Allow about 15 minutes. In many social and business situations people ask 'What do you do?' First think about how you currently answer, e.g. 'I'm a teacher', 'I make architectural models', 'I'm in accounts'. Then watch Sinek apply 'start with why' to himself.

blocks.title: Video 3 Start with why: answering the question 'What do you do?'
blocks.note: Simon Sinek focuses his 'start with why' approach on himself, showing how to answer 'What do you do?' by starting with why you do it.

blocks.title: Activity 1 'What do you do?'
blocks.prompt: Part 1: Write how you currently answer the question 'What do you do?'. Part 2: Taking Simon Sinek's advice into account, write a new answer that starts with why you do what you do.
blocks.model: In marketing language you are starting to develop your 'elevator pitch' - typically two or three short sentences explaining who you are and what you do. If you focus on 'why' you do it, as Sinek suggests, you should receive an even more positive response. Focus on what you do now; later in the course you can decide whether to change it, and in Week 8 you'll revisit the elevator pitch.
points: Gives a current 'what I do' answer
Rewrites the answer to start with why they do it
Keeps it short, like a two or three sentence elevator pitch
Focuses on what they do now

blocks.text: In a corporate context, company values describe what an organisation stands for. They are typically kept to four or five and are usually communicated through actions and words.
Research by communications consultancy Maitland (Marinker, 2015) looked at the stated core values of FTSE 100 companies. The top 10 were:

items: Integrity
Respect
Innovation
Safety
Transparency
Excellence
Team work
Honesty
Trust
Responsibility

blocks.alt: 'Core values' written in chalk on a board, surrounded by words such as trust, quality, integrity, innovation, ethics and respect
blocks.caption: Figure 2 Core values

blocks.text: The Maitland report notes that 'so many of the more commonly expressed values relate to behaviour traits rather than strategic or operational characteristics' and that 'Most people will consider these to be universally desirable behaviours rather than distinctive and informative glimpses into corporate culture' (Marinker, 2015, pp.4, 8).

blocks.title: Applying this to you
blocks.text: Aim for a mix of behavioural and operational characteristics. Employers value integrity and respect, but they also want to know your operationally useful skills, such as problem solving or strategic thinking. If your brand is the same as everyone else's, how will you stand out?
Some companies don't demonstrate the values they claim to stand for! If you present yourself in a certain way, make sure you can live up to that image.

blocks.q: What did the Maitland report observe about the most commonly stated FTSE 100 values?
options: They mostly describe strategic and operational characteristics
They mostly relate to behaviour traits seen as universally desirable
They are usually unique to each company
blocks.explain: Most were behaviour traits that people see as universally desirable, rather than distinctive glimpses into corporate culture.

blocks.text: Allow about 10 minutes. Think of a brand you admire and identify its values - most companies list them on their website. For example:

blocks.title: Activity 2 Brand values
blocks.prompt: Write a short paragraph or bullet list of the ways your chosen brand demonstrates or communicates its values in what it does or says.
blocks.model: Your brand might communicate its values through the quality of its products, its approach to sustainability or its commitment to innovation. The Design Council notes that values are hard to communicate: overt marketing may seem disingenuous, while not communicating them may mean people don't see what you stand for, and any values must be genuine and upheld in how the organisation operates. Methods include graphic design, language, advertising, staff training and the materials used in products.
points: Identifies the values of a chosen brand
Gives examples of how the brand shows those values in actions or words
Recognises values must be genuine and upheld in practice
Mentions methods such as design, language, advertising or staff training

blocks.text: When a company's brand values are clearly communicated, they attract people who share those values and who become core customers. They may even become brand advocates, sharing the brand with others and encouraging them to find out more.

This transfers to personal branding: attracting the attention of like-minded colleagues and peers ensures your reputation spreads in the right way. Later in the course you'll look at tools for sharing your values, such as a CV or a social media post.

blocks.title: Brand advocate
blocks.text: Someone who shares a brand's values and actively recommends it to others.
Brand vision is the concept whereby a business strategically plans where and how its brand will be positioned at some point in the future, e.g. 5 or 10 years from now.
Microsoft was founded with a vision of a computer on every desk, and in every home. We've never wavered from that vision.

In the 40 years since, Microsoft has made significant progress towards achieving it! For you, a vision of where you want your career to be in, say, five years helps you define and communicate your brand. If you want a new employer, you'll need to reach a wider audience than for internal promotion. A vision should be just out of reach; regularly re-evaluate your progress and ambitions so it can change as your career develops.

blocks.alt: The Microsoft logo on a sign at the entrance to its head office
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Microsoft premises

pages.title: Personality: how do you come across?

blocks.text: Brand personality is all about the human characteristics that can be attributed to a brand. The Design Council explains: 'Personality traits could be efficient and business-like, friendly and chatty, or perhaps humorous and irreverent' (Design Council, n.d.).
This aligns strongly with personal branding. You won't need to make up characteristics - they are your own - but you *will* need to choose which ones to highlight and showcase.

Personality can show in the language and tone used to promote a brand, or even in the colour of its logo. You won't usually need a logo, but it's interesting to consider what colour best represents you and the brand you want to develop.

pages.title: Activity 3 What colour is my brand?

blocks.text: Allow about 5 minutes. Boutique Media Communication's infographic shows what different colours might suggest about a brand.

blocks.alt: Infographic of seven colour columns - red, pink, purple, navy, green, blue, orange - each listing associated words and example brand logos. Red: passionate, active, bold, confidence, power (Kellogg's, Coca-Cola, LEGO). Pink: love, respect, warmth, nurture (Barbie). Purple: creativity, original, individual, compassion (Cadbury). Navy: trust, loyalty, authority, success (Facebook). Green: balance, growth, clarity, prosperity (BP, Starbucks). Blue: spirit, control, determination, ambition (Intel, Skype). Orange: instinct, warmth, optimistic, social, freedom (Fanta, Orange).
blocks.caption: Figure 4 Colour infographic

blocks.title: Activity 3 What colour is my brand?
blocks.prompt: Look at the characteristics associated with each colour and decide which one best represents your own personal brand. Write the colour and say why.
blocks.model: This is a fun look at another aspect of branding. If you respond well to visual content, having a colour in mind can help when thinking about your brand - someone who identifies with red might present themselves very differently from someone aligned with green. A colour can also be practical, for example if you promote your brand through social media such as Facebook or Instagram.
points: Chooses a colour
Links the colour to characteristics they identify with
Considers how the colour could be used practically, e.g. on social media

blocks.text: Marketing and branding professionals spend significant time on target audience. Failing to identify the correct audience risks wasting time and money, attracting the wrong audience, or creating communications too generic to be effective.
Focusing on small businesses, Blick (2013, pp.42-44) explains that reaching your target audience is a two-stage process:

items: **Identifying it** - considering the type of customer group your business will appeal to. The smaller the target group, the more manageable it is to reach.
**Researching it** - getting to know the target audience before you start to communicate with it.

blocks.alt: A hand circles a small group of white figures on a screen with a red pen
blocks.caption: Figure 5 Target audience

blocks.text: The process applies equally to personal branding. Many employers might suit your brand, so how can you narrow them down to make communicating with them manageable? Blick's practical questions (p.43) can be adapted to employers you'd like to work for:

items: Will you only target certain postcodes, towns, counties, etc.?
Do you only want to target businesses of a certain size?
Can you be more specific about the type of business? If you've identified 'schools', can you narrow that to certain types of school?

blocks.q: According to Blick, the larger the target group, the more manageable it becomes to reach them.
blocks.explain: Blick says the smaller the target group, the more manageable it becomes to reach them.

blocks.text: Blick also suggests research methods (pp.44-45) that are equally relevant to personal branding:

items: Search online for forums or blogs your target audience belongs to (or co-ordinates/produces)
Subscribe to publications your target audience reads
Call businesses you'd like to connect with - in a personal context, ask where they advertise vacancies or what skills they are short of
Find out if your audience belongs to a membership organisation or group with events or conferences you could attend

blocks.text: If you know what an organisation is looking for, whether it matches what you offer, and who the key people are, you can significantly enhance your chances. In recruitment, the more targeted and well-researched your application, the more likely you are to be invited to interview.
Allow about 10 minutes.

blocks.title: Case study: Tara
blocks.text: Tara is unhappy at work and wants to change direction but has no idea where to start. She is a retail assistant in a high street clothing store but would love to be a landscape gardener. She has GCSEs but no relevant gardening qualifications. Her experience comes from gardening at home and volunteering to help maintain the plants in a local park.

blocks.title: Activity 4 Tara's target audience
blocks.prompt: Referring to Blick's advice on identifying and researching a target audience, what would you suggest Tara does next? Write a bullet-pointed list.
blocks.model: Tara could decide whether to stay where she is or move, and list potential employers in her chosen locations. She could subscribe to relevant publications and join blogs and forums on landscape gardening to learn about employment and gain contacts. She could contact garden centres, plant nurseries and landscape gardening companies to ask what jobs suit her experience and where they advertise, and ask for work experience or advice on courses and qualifications. After this research she'll have a much better idea of her next move.
points: Narrow down location and list potential employers
Subscribe to publications and join online blogs or forums
Contact relevant employers to ask about suitable jobs and where they advertise
Ask for work experience or advice on courses and qualifications

blocks.text: Once the brand and audience are clear, the marketing professionals' next step is brand positioning.

blocks.title: Brand positioning
blocks.text: 'the act of designing the company's offering and image to occupy a distinctive place in the mind of the target market' (Kotler and Keller, 2003, p.867).

The Branding Journal (Marion, n.d.) adds that 'brand positioning describes how a brand is different from its competitors and where, or how, it sits in customers' minds. A brand positioning strategy therefore involves creating brand associations in customers' minds to make them perceive the brand in a specific way.'

blocks.alt: Many orange squares drawn on a blackboard, with a hand drawing a white circle in a small gap between them
blocks.caption: Figure 6 Making your brand stand out

blocks.text: Brand taglines from past and present illustrate different ways a brand might be positioned:

head: Focus
Examples
rows: Volvo: 'For life'; M&Ms: 'Melts in your mouth and not in your hand'
Facebook: 'Helps you connect and share with the people in your life'; Sainsbury's: 'Live well for less'
On how the company does business
Audi: 'Vorsprung durch Technik' (Advancement through technology); Burger King: 'Have it your way'
Apple: 'Think different'; Avis: 'We're #2. We try harder'

blocks.text: Table 1 Examples of brand positioning, adapted from equibrandconsulting.com. As the more concise messages of social media marketing grow, taglines are used less, but this categorisation is useful for your own brand.
Applying the four categories to your personal brand, you might:

items: emphasise the **benefits** an employer will gain from hiring you - highlighting the skills, knowledge and experience you bring to a role
focus on the employer as a **consumer** and explain how you can make their life easier
explain how you 'do **business**', e.g. showcasing your values and how they align with the organisation's
clarify the ways you are better than your **competitors** - without appearing mean or overly competitive, as that can backfire

blocks.title: Match each tagline to its positioning focus

pairs.def: M&Ms: 'Melts in your mouth and not in your hand'
Sainsbury's: 'Live well for less'

pairs.term: Focus on how the company does business
pairs.def: Burger King: 'Have it your way'
Avis: 'We're #2. We try harder'

blocks.text: Allow about 15 minutes. Don't spend too long thinking - just write down any words that spring to mind.

blocks.title: Activity 5 My own brand perceptions
blocks.prompt: List your observations of these well-known brands: 1. Apple, 2. Amazon, 3. Tesco. Then reflect: were your perceptions negative or positive? Were they based on personal experience or on advertising? Did they change once you experienced the brand?
blocks.model: Once you have personal experience of a brand, your perceptions rest on many things, from interactions with staff to product reliability. Before that, you are more likely to be influenced by branding messages. The same applies to employers: until they meet you, they only have your application, social media posts and what others say about you, so present your brand in a way that encourages them to get in touch.
points: Gives words for Apple, Amazon and Tesco
Notes whether perceptions are positive or negative
Distinguishes personal experience from advertising messages
Links this to how employers perceive you before meeting you

blocks.text: Once a company has positioned its brand, it must ensure its messages are consistent. Big brands know that delivering a consistent brand is crucial in winning customers' trust, so they present the same message over and over. Customers who know and trust a brand are more likely to show brand loyalty and become effective brand ambassadors.

blocks.alt: A spanner with the word 'consistency' written on it lies in the centre of a pile of tools
blocks.caption: Figure 7 Consistency is an important tool

blocks.q: Customers who know and trust a brand are more likely to show brand loyalty and become brand ambassadors.
blocks.explain: Consistency wins trust, and trust leads to loyalty and ambassadorship.

blocks.text: William Arruda (2016) uses Starbucks as an example:

What would you think if you walked into a Starbucks and the barista got your triple tall, half caf, iced, non-fat latte wrong? You'd probably say to yourself, "First-world problem," not fret too much and go about your day. What if you went to a different location the next day, and your order was mishandled once again? Part of the brand promise of Starbucks is that you'll receive a customized beverage that perfectly suits your palate and your diet, no matter how complex the details or your order are. How many times would you be willing to experience inconsistency before you switched to a different caffeine dealer?

blocks.alt: A white Starbucks cup next to a pile of coffee beans
blocks.caption: Figure 8 Starbucks coffee

blocks.text: Arruda points out that consistency doesn't mean you can't change anything. The Virgin brand's history includes:

items: 1960s - a student magazine
1970s - record stores and a record label
1980s - video games, an airline, holidays, balloon flights and hotels
1990s - a radio station and cinemas
2000s - trains and a mobile phone network
2010s - space travel and banking!

blocks.text: What remains consistent are its brand values - 'providing heartfelt service, being delightfully surprising, red hot, and straight up while maintaining an insatiable curiosity and creating smart disruption' - and its purpose, 'changing business for good' (Virgin, 2018).

blocks.alt: The red tail of a Virgin aeroplane against a blue sky with white clouds
blocks.caption: Figure 9 Virgin airline

blocks.text: Allow about 5 minutes. Think back to Activity 3 in Week 1, when you asked three people to describe you in three words.

blocks.title: Activity 6 Consistent messages
blocks.prompt: List the words the three people used. Did each of them use the same or similar words, or were they different? If different, why might that be?
blocks.model: Similar words indicate your brand messages are consistent; next consider whether they are the right words for the brand you want to convey (Week 4 looks at the key elements of your brand). Different words may be because people know you in different contexts - many of us have a different workplace persona from the 'real' one we show friends and family. Is there something you could do to make those personas more aligned?
points: Lists the words others used
Judges whether the words were consistent
Considers whether they are the right words for the desired brand
Reflects on different personas at work and at home and how to align them

blocks.text: Being consistent matters equally in what you say and what you do, and the two should be closely aligned. When people start to trust you, your personal brand is working and new career opportunities will arise.
Now that you've completed Week 2, take this short quiz to reflect on what you've learned.

blocks.q: Which is NOT one of the Design Council's 'four cornerstones' of a good brand?
blocks.explain: The four cornerstones are the big idea, values, vision and personality.

blocks.q: What does Simon Sinek's Golden Circle model say successful organisations focus on communicating?
options: Why they do what they do
blocks.explain: Sinek's 'start with why' approach focuses on why an organisation does what it does.

blocks.q: What are Blick's two stages for successfully reaching your target audience?
options: Advertising it and selling to it
Competing for it and keeping it
blocks.explain: Blick (2013) describes identifying the target audience, then researching it before communicating with it.

blocks.q: Kotler and Keller define brand positioning as designing the offering and image to...
options: occupy a distinctive place in the mind of the target market
match competitors as closely as possible
blocks.explain: Positioning is 'the act of designing the company's offering and image to occupy a distinctive place in the mind of the target market'.

blocks.q: What does the Virgin example show about brand consistency?
options: A consistent brand must never change its products
Products can change while values and purpose stay consistent
Consistency only matters for coffee shops
blocks.explain: Virgin moved from magazines to space travel and banking, but its values and purpose stayed consistent.

blocks.q: A brand vision should be easily achievable within a year.
blocks.explain: A vision is a plan for where the brand will be in perhaps 5 or 10 years, and should always be just out of reach - something to strive for.

blocks.text: This week demonstrated some of the core principles and practices involved in successfully marketing a product or organisation. As this is more familiar territory than personal branding, the consumer context introduced themes you'll consider in later weeks.
You've considered the key elements of a strong brand, looked at how to identify a target audience and explored brand positioning and the importance of consistent messages.
You should now be able to:

items: describe the key elements of a successful brand
appreciate the concept of target audience
recognise the importance of positioning a brand correctly

cards.back: The big idea, values, vision and personality (Design Council).
A strategic plan of where and how a brand will be positioned in the future, e.g. 5 or 10 years from now.
The human characteristics that can be attributed to a brand.
The group a brand aims to reach - identified, then researched (Blick, 2013).
Designing the offering and image to occupy a distinctive place in the mind of the target market (Kotler and Keller).

blocks.text: Next week you will look at the development and use of personal branding in more detail.

chapters.title: Week 3: Personal branding explained
chapters.summary: How personal branding developed, how a clear brand helps at work, what to learn from celebrity brands, and why authenticity matters.

blocks.text: Last week you were introduced to the processes and practices behind branding a product or organisation, and started to consider how they might be applied in a personal branding context.
This week you'll look at personal branding in more detail: how and why it has developed, and what can be learned from those who use their personal brand effectively, or not.

blocks.title: Video 1 Introduction to Week 3
blocks.note: A short animated introduction with no spoken audio. Personal branding is still a relatively new concept. In the 1990s Tom Peters said 'It's this simple. You are a brand. You are in charge of your brand.' The impact of social media has been huge. This week focuses on how a strong personal brand can make a difference in the workplace, what you can learn from the way celebrities use and manipulate their brands, and what happens when mistakes are made - and how to avoid them happening to you.

blocks.text: By the end of this week, you will be able to:

items: recognise how a clear personal brand can be beneficial to your career
appreciate the ways that celebrity branding tactics might be used to your own advantage
understand the value of developing an authentic brand.

blocks.text: When considering the origins of personal branding, authors often quote Socrates, who said: 'The way to gain a good reputation is to endeavour to be what you desire to appear' (Karaduman 2013, p.465).

blocks.alt: The word BRAND written in red on white, surrounded by sketched words such as research, identity, strategy, trust, design and teamwork.
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Brand is important

blocks.text: In the 1950s, sociologist Erving Goffman first published *The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life*, which suggested that we spend our lives playing a series of different parts in order to present ourselves to others in the best possible light.

blocks.title: Video 2 Erving Goffman's work
blocks.note: A short clip explaining Goffman's work on the presentation of self in more detail.

blocks.text: Following his 1997 article, 'The Brand Called You', many authors refer to Tom Peters as the 'father of personal branding'. He closes the article with this call to action:

It's this simple: You are a brand. You are in charge of your brand. There is no single path to success. And there is no one right way to create the brand called You. Except this: Start today. Or else.

This viewpoint was ground-breaking over 20 years ago, but personal branding is now a familiar concept. It has grown in popularity following the explosion of the internet, combined with a desire to prioritise job satisfaction and a need to stand out in an increasingly competitive job market.

Before the internet, the first people to use personal branding to their advantage were celebrities and other professionals with a public profile, such as politicians. They used television, radio and newspapers, or made appearances at events, giving speeches and meeting people.

blocks.title: Activity 1 How things have changed (about 10 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Imagine a politician campaigning to win an election in the 1990s, before the internet and social media became ubiquitous. If you were in their marketing team, how might you promote their personal brand? Which media would you use, and how would you make sure their messages reached the maximum number of people? Now fast forward to today: how would your promotional campaign differ? Note your thoughts for the 1990s and for now.
blocks.model: In the 1990s and before, politicians had to rely on inspiring oration and personal charisma. Appearing at key events, giving speeches and shaking lots of hands allowed people to see and hear what they had to say, and newspaper, radio or television coverage broadened their reach, as it still does today. Now social media has changed all that: a politician doesn't even need to leave their office to reach millions. Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, etc. get their message directly into the homes of potential voters, reaching the younger generations they most want to influence.
points: In the 1990s politicians relied on speeches, events, personal charisma and meeting people.
Newspapers, radio and television broadened their reach.
Today social media lets them reach millions without leaving the office.
Social media puts messages directly into voters' homes and reaches younger generations.

pages.title: Personal branding is not 'me me me'

blocks.text: The impact of the internet and social media on personal branding has been huge. But this has also led to a common misinterpretation of what personal branding is. Arruda (2017) explains:

...personal branding works when it is based in authenticity and a genuine desire to add value to those around you. It is not a 'me me me' way of life. Personal branding does allow you to stand out in an increasingly competitive world. It helps you clarify and express the value you can deliver to your team and employer. Personal branding is not a competition to see how visible you can become - for the sake of being visible.
Arruda laments that 'conflating personal branding with social media excess has eroded the true value of personal branding as a serious career development strategy'.

blocks.q: According to Arruda, the strength of a personal brand is measured by how visible you are on social media.
blocks.explain: Arruda says personal branding is not a competition to be visible for the sake of it, nor measured in tweets per minute; it works when based on authenticity and a genuine desire to add value to others.

blocks.text: Paying attention to your personal brand at work can have an impact in two key areas:

items: You are better prepared to present a clear message to others about who you are and what you have to offer.
Colleagues, peers and employers will have a clear understanding of what they can gain from working with you.

blocks.text: Sometimes you might want to boost your personal brand image in the workplace because you are facing a challenging situation and want to demonstrate that you can deal with it.

blocks.title: Video 3 Interview with Jane Chapman
blocks.note: Business Image Consultant Jane Chapman explains how image can enhance your authority in a challenging work context. 1) Think about the psychology of colour: dark neutrals (navy, charcoal grey, black) automatically give you more gravitas - base your outfit on them and add a bit of other colour, rather than black head to toe. 2) Wear something you feel 'a million dollars' in and comfortable in, so you don't have to think about it. 3) Wear something that makes you feel confident - typically dressing a bit smarter. Body language: avoid closed body language where you shrink down; think about eye contact and projecting confidence. When you look like you can handle anything, chances are you'll feel confident enough to do it.

blocks.text: Jane Chapman's advice gives some simple, practical ways to project confidence when the pressure is on.

blocks.q: Which of these does Jane Chapman suggest will give you more gravitas in a challenging work situation?
options: Wearing bright colours from head to toe
Basing your outfit on a dark neutral such as navy or charcoal
Dressing down so you seem approachable
blocks.explain: She says dark neutrals automatically give you more gravitas, but recommends adding a bit of other colour rather than wearing black head to toe; dressing a bit smarter usually builds confidence.

blocks.text: Leya had been working as a careers adviser for five years when her boss suggested she try managing a department for a few months while a colleague was seconded elsewhere. Management was not something Leya had ever considered, but her boss was sure she would excel. She accepted, found she really enjoyed the role, and is now the Director of a large careers service.

blocks.title: Why it happened
blocks.text: Leya had developed a clear personal brand within the organisation. She was known for her strong interpersonal skills and her ability to motivate and encourage others. She hadn't deliberately cultivated a brand, but by being open and honest in all her interactions with colleagues and clients, her personal brand was authentic and clear for all to see.

Linda had been a manager for several years when she applied for a job that seemed to require her skillset but included oversight of many operational areas she knew little about. At interview, she decided to be clear about who she was and what she could offer, rather than apologising for gaps in her knowledge. She focused on her track record of working with a wide range of people, bringing them together and building effective teams. She got the job!

blocks.title: Why it worked
blocks.text: The authentic brand Linda communicated was exactly what the employer was looking for. Unknown to her, there had been significant personnel issues and the team was fractured and aimless. By presenting her brand clearly and confidently, she convinced the employer she was the perfect person to sort that out.

pages.title: Case study: Philip's social media marketing

blocks.text: When Philip left a senior role to start a freelance career, he wanted the right people to know he was available. He developed a website, thinking carefully about how to present himself, then focused on LinkedIn and Twitter - regularly posting thoughts and ideas and commenting on other material. He had always done this, but now did it more deliberately, considering how his comments might be perceived by potential employers and keeping them regular and timely. Offers of work followed!

For Philip this wasn't about collecting followers or a target of five tweets a day. He wanted the right people to notice and remember him for the right, professional reasons. Once his brand was valued, he could approach followers directly with ideas about how he could help them - and his pitches were well received because his reputation was already strong.
Gayle Johnson is a self-employed copywriter and coach who took a more deliberate approach to defining her personal brand at work.

blocks.title: Video 4 Interview with Gayle Johnson
blocks.note: As a middle manager in a large university facing many competing demands and change programmes, Gayle realised that you can't control everything, but you can control what you stand for. She became more conscious and deliberate about how she showed up at work - not putting on a mask, but bringing out what she really stood for and her values. Being herself gave her confidence and strength, made her more effective (no energy wasted on a mask) and strengthened her relationships and network of trusted people. Later she realised the job couldn't fulfil her further, so she set up her own copywriting and writing-mentor business. With thousands of competitors and the belief that 'people buy people', she was very deliberate about being herself and letting people into her world. Three years on, she only works with clients she really connects with, who value what she does.

blocks.title: Key point
blocks.text: Gayle's brand helped her feel more authentic, which boosted her job satisfaction and professional relationships.

pages.title: Activity 2 How could personal branding help me at work?

blocks.title: Activity 2 How could personal branding help me at work? (about 15 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Think about your current work situation. How is your personal brand working for you at the moment? Has it brought you any unexpected opportunities, as it did for Leya? Choose one thing you are happy with about your brand and one thing you'd like to improve. You might find it helpful to look back at Week 1, Activity 3, where you asked others to describe you.
blocks.model: Leya didn't consciously develop a personal brand at work, but others recognised it because of her consistent actions and behaviour. Gayle had a clear idea of why a strong brand mattered to her, and developing it helped her feel more authentic, enhancing her job satisfaction and professional relationships. Week 1, Activity 3 might have shown how your brand is currently perceived. You can now consider whether to alter or enhance it - for example, promoting a particular strength or set of values more strongly, or simply wanting more people to know and recognise your brand.
points: Name one thing about your current brand you are happy with.
Name one thing you would like to improve or promote more strongly.
A brand can be recognised through consistent actions and behaviour, even if not deliberately built.
An authentic brand can improve job satisfaction and work relationships.

pages.title: What can I learn from celebrity branding?

blocks.text: For most of us, personal branding brings certain celebrities to mind. Their brands are cultivated deliberately to maximise their following and the potential profit from appearances, product ranges and endorsements. But what can we learn from their approach for our own careers?

blocks.alt: A glamorous woman in a black dress steps out of a car onto a red carpet as photographers crowd around with flashes going off.
blocks.caption: Figure 2 The red carpet

blocks.text: 1 A clearly defined brand

The brands of talk show host and philanthropist Oprah Winfrey, or singer-songwriter Lady Gaga, are clearly defined and come across as authentic: we know what they do and what they stand for. Take time to identify your own authentic brand, starting with questions such as 'What are my values?' or 'What do I want to be known for?'

pages.title: Sharing your brand and making connections

blocks.text: 2 Share your brand through a variety of channels

Celebrities broaden their profile by endorsing existing products to reach new audiences - for example David Beckham's endorsement of watches and whisky, or Justin Timberlake co-founding a clothing line with an established designer. You might start a blog or volunteer to present at a meeting or conference.
3 Connect with other brands

Singers duet with other famous singers (e.g. David Bowie and Bing Crosby's 'Peace on Earth'/'Little Drummer Boy'), and actors perform together in fund-raising events such as Comic Relief. You could write a guest blog for someone whose audience you can connect with, or present your work to another department. The key point is expanding your network.
4 Successful celebrity brands have clear boundaries

Many celebrities have struggled with what to post on social media or how to respond to negative comments - some have withdrawn altogether. Those with the most successful brands have clear boundaries about how much they will share and what they will or won't respond to.

Social media can reach a much wider audience, but decide how you want to use it rather than feeling pressurised to have an online profile. Ask yourself: 'Will it help me to achieve what I want in my career, or are there other methods that might be more effective?'

blocks.title: Focus
blocks.text: If you use social media, focus on one tool rather than spreading yourself across every platform. LinkedIn is an obvious one for many professionals, but Instagram might fit your brand and ambitions better. You'll look at promoting your brand online in Week 6.

blocks.title: Match each celebrity tactic to how you could adapt it

pairs.def: Ask yourself 'What are my values?' and 'What do I want to be known for?'

pairs.term: Sharing through a variety of channels
pairs.def: Start a blog or volunteer to present at a meeting or conference
Write a guest blog for someone with an audience you can connect with
Decide how much to share online and what you will or won't respond to

blocks.text: JK Rowling, author of the Harry Potter books, is a regular user of Twitter. Read these tweets (or use a public figure you follow):

items: 'It's that anniversary again. This year, I apologise for killing someone who didn't die during the #BattleofHogwarts, but who laid down his life to save the people who'd win it. I refer, of course, to Dobby the house elf.'
'Argentinian artist Marta Minujín's monumental replica of the Greek Parthenon created with 100,000 copies of banned books, to [sic] symbolizes the resistance to political repression #womensart'
'You're free to offend. The rest of us are free to say we're offended. That's what freedom of speech means.'
'Your regular reminder that @AlabedBana is the girl who live tweeted as bombs fell, while pro-Assad apologists claimed she didn't exist.'

blocks.title: Activity 3 Using social media (about 10 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Based on these four tweets, describe your impression of JK Rowling's personal brand.
blocks.model: You might have picked up that she is (a) caring and appreciative - apologising to fans for something unpopular in a novel, while referring to an exciting event that might entice new readers; (b) a champion for the repressed - using her celebrity to showcase women's art; (c) strong willed - responding to detractors and clear about what she believes; and (d) not afraid of expressing her opinions, with strong political views. Her tweets are consistent and clearly reflect her personal brand, so readers can decide whether they support or disagree with her. In a career context, your tweets can similarly affect how an employer perceives you and whether they want to work with you.
points: She comes across as caring and appreciative of her fans.
She champions the repressed and showcases causes such as women's art.
She is strong willed and not afraid to express her opinions.
Her tweets are consistent and clearly reflect her brand.
Your own posts can affect how employers perceive you.

blocks.text: Oprah Winfrey is a talk show host, actor, philanthropist and owner of a multi-media production company. The Cult Branding Company (n.d.) summarises her brand:

Some TV personalities seem distant and removed from the general public, but Oprah has never shied away from sharing intimate, personal details about her life with her audience. [...] She is indeed an ordinary person with ordinary problems to overcome. It's her seeming vulnerability and fragility that make her that much more inclusive of a brand.

blocks.alt: President Barack Obama places the Presidential Medal of Freedom on a blue ribbon around Oprah Winfrey's neck.
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Oprah Winfrey receiving the Presidential Medal of Freedom

blocks.text: Sharing that level of detail would be uncomfortable for most of us, and usually unnecessary in a career context, but the case clearly illustrates the value of an authentic brand.

The concept of an authentic or 'true' self is contentious. Some authors see it as relevant and important; others describe it as a non-scientific 'fiction' (Strohminger, 2017, p.7). Strohminger gives two reasons:

items: 'the true self depends on the values of the observer' and is therefore subjective 'and strongly tied to what each individual person herself most prizes', and
'claims made on its behalf may completely contradict all available data', so 'the true self is posited rather than observed'.

blocks.text: While the existence of an authentic self might not be scientifically proven, the word 'authentic' is regularly used when discussing personal branding because it presents a useful and relevant concept.
Positive psychology professor Stephen Joseph (2016) lists common characteristics of authentic and inauthentic people:

head: Authentic
Inauthentic
rows: Are self-deceptive and unrealistic in their perceptions of reality
Are accepting of themselves and of other people
Look to others for approval and to feel valued
Express their emotions freely and clearly
Are unable to express their emotions freely and clearly
Are open to learning from their mistakes
Are not open to learning from their mistakes

blocks.text: Table 1, adapted from Joseph (2016). He explains: 'If behind what a person says and does is a defensive and self-deceptive approach to life, then no matter how passionate and committed they are to a cause, ultimately they are not being true to themselves.'
Use Joseph's table to check your understanding.

blocks.q: According to Joseph (2016), which of these are characteristics of *authentic* people? Select all that apply.
options: They look to others for approval to feel valued
They are open to learning from their mistakes
They are judgemental of other people
They accept themselves and other people
blocks.explain: Authentic people are realistic, self-accepting and accepting of others, thoughtful, emotionally expressive, open to learning from mistakes and understand their motivations. Seeking approval and judging others are inauthentic traits.

blocks.title: Video 5 Simon Sinek on how authentic behaviour builds trust
blocks.note: Respected author and motivational speaker Simon Sinek explains authenticity: authentic behaviour builds trust, and it means ensuring that you believe in the things you say and do.

blocks.title: Activity 4 Can I be authentic at work? (about 15 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Based on what Simon Sinek said about believing in the things you say and do, ask yourself: (1) Are there times when I must do things that go against my own values? For example, you really value family but must work long hours and always feel you're neglecting them. (2) Do I ever have to work in a way that doesn't reflect my preferred style? For example, your job requires you to focus on the bigger picture when you'd prefer to immerse yourself in operational detail.
blocks.model: If your work doesn't align with your values or preferred style and you must present yourself in a way that feels inauthentic, that can affect your job satisfaction. The Kaleidoscope Career Model (Mainiero & Sullivan, 2006), from a five-year study of career patterns, identifies three parameters that lead people to take stock and make career changes: a need for challenge, a need for balance, and a need to ask 'How can I be authentic, true to myself and make genuine decisions for myself?' We all compromise sometimes, but compromising too much can affect your satisfaction, your attitude to your job and how others perceive your brand.
points: Identify any times work conflicts with your values.
Identify any ways you work against your preferred style.
Feeling inauthentic at work can reduce job satisfaction.
The Kaleidoscope Career Model names challenge, balance and authenticity as drivers of career change.
Too much compromise can affect how others perceive your brand.

blocks.text: Discussions about the 'authentic self' will undoubtedly continue. For the purposes of this course, it may help to think of authenticity as meaning 'genuine, real and true'.

blocks.title: Authenticity
blocks.text: Genuine, real and true. The more honest you can be in presenting your personal brand, the more effective it will be in representing who you are and what you are looking for.

blocks.title: Kaleidoscope Career Model
blocks.text: Mainiero & Sullivan (2006): people take stock of their careers and make transitions to meet three needs - **challenge**, **balance** and **authenticity**.

Several celebrities have aligned themselves with products or campaigns that harmed their personal brand. In 2014, actress Scarlett Johansson, known for supporting charities and at the time an Oxfam ambassador, signed a contract to promote Sodastream. The company is headquartered in Israel and had a factory in an Israeli settlement on the West Bank.

Oxfam wrote to her explaining that it 'believes that businesses that operate in settlements further the ongoing poverty and denial of rights of the Palestinian communities that we work to support'. She stood by her decision and eventually stepped down from her Oxfam role (Thorpe, 2014).

blocks.alt: A woman sits at her desk in front of a computer, glasses in hand, rubbing her eyes in frustration.
blocks.caption: Figure 4 When your personal brand goes wrong

blocks.text: More recently, supermodel and TV personality Kendall Jenner made a Pepsi advert in which she handed a can of the drink to a riot policeman at a protest. Given the #BlackLivesMatter protests in the US at the time, the public felt it was an inappropriate subject for a soft drink advert and there was widespread condemnation (Sanghani, 2017). The company apologised and cancelled the advert.
Neither career suffered lasting damage, but both had to deal with negative feedback and may have lost credibility with some followers.

blocks.title: Lessons for you
blocks.text: Think about what or who you align yourself with: do they fit the personal brand you wish to promote? Make sure the views you share with colleagues, social media followers, etc. represent your brand effectively.
Webber (n.d.) discusses common mistakes people make with their personal branding:

items: **You haven't clarified your purpose** - first decide exactly who you want to be, then start self-promoting.
**You're not sharing the right things** - are you over- or under-promoting, or being careless about what you share?
**You're caught up in the career you've already had, not the one you want** - choose the projects and experiences you'd most like to replicate and talk about them.

blocks.q: According to Webber, what should you do *before* you start self-promoting?
options: Build as large a following as possible
Decide exactly who you want to be
List every job you have ever had
Copy the brand of a successful celebrity
blocks.explain: Webber's first mistake is not clarifying your purpose: decide exactly who you want to be, then start promoting yourself.

pages.title: Activity 5 It doesn't work for me

blocks.title: Activity 5 It doesn't work for me (about 10 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Think of a person in the public eye with a high-profile personal brand you really don't align with - a reality TV star, politician, actor, etc. Summarise why their personal brand doesn't work for you. Then list what other people do like about them.
blocks.model: This person's high-profile brand shows that even though you don't feel aligned with them, others clearly do. Perhaps they made obvious mistakes that put you off, or their brand simply doesn't attract or interest you. The point is that you can never devise a personal brand that will appeal to everyone. If you are brave enough to share the authentic you with the world, you must accept that some negativity is likely to come your way - and that's fine. Those who do buy into your values will be the people you most enjoy talking to and working with.
points: Explain why this person's brand doesn't appeal to you.
Identify what other people like about them.
No personal brand can appeal to everyone.
Being authentic means accepting some negativity.
The people who share your values are the ones you'll most enjoy working with.

blocks.title: Match each idea to its source

pairs.def: The way to gain a good reputation is to endeavour to be what you desire to appear
We play a series of parts to present ourselves to others in the best possible light
You are a brand. You are in charge of your brand. Start today.
Personal branding is not a 'me me me' way of life or a competition to be visible
The true self is posited rather than observed
Authentic people are open to learning from their mistakes and understand their motivations

blocks.text: Reflect on what you've learned this week.

blocks.q: Who is often called the 'father of personal branding'?
blocks.explain: Following his 1997 article 'The Brand Called You', many authors refer to Tom Peters as the father of personal branding.

blocks.q: Why was Leya offered the chance to manage a department?
options: She had deliberately marketed herself on social media
She had a clear, authentic brand built on openness and honesty, known for interpersonal and motivational skills
She applied for a management qualification
She had the longest service in the team
blocks.explain: Leya hadn't cultivated a brand deliberately; her open, honest interactions made her strengths in interpersonal skills and motivating others clear to everyone.

blocks.q: Philip's social media approach was mainly about collecting as many followers as possible.
blocks.explain: Philip wanted the right people to notice and remember him for the right, professional reasons, not to collect followers or hit tweet targets.

blocks.q: What is the key point of connecting your brand with others (e.g. guest blogging, presenting to another department)?
blocks.explain: Celebrities duet or appear together to broaden awareness; for you the key point is expanding your network.

blocks.q: What broad lesson does the course draw from the Scarlett Johansson and Kendall Jenner cases?
options: Think about what or who you align yourself with and whether it fits your brand
Negative feedback always ends a career
Only share views on social media
blocks.explain: Neither suffered lasting career damage, but both faced negative feedback; the lesson is to check that what you align with and the views you share fit your brand.

blocks.q: A well-designed personal brand can appeal to everyone.
blocks.explain: You can never devise a personal brand that appeals to everyone; being authentic means accepting some negativity.

blocks.text: This week you focused on real-life examples of personal branding and looked at the impact it can have in the workplace. You considered what can be learned from the personal branding of people in the public eye, and how their approach can be applied by those of us who don't aspire to celebrity!
You should now be able to:

items: recognise how a clear personal brand can be beneficial to your career
appreciate the ways that celebrity branding tactics might be used to your own advantage
understand the value of developing an authentic brand.

cards.back: Tom Peters' 1997 article; he is often called the 'father of personal branding'.
Genuine, real and true - the more honest your brand, the more effective it is.
Mainiero & Sullivan (2006): career changes are driven by needs for challenge, balance and authenticity.
Conflating personal branding with social media excess erodes its value as a career strategy.
Not clarifying purpose; not sharing the right things; focusing on the career you've had, not the one you want.

blocks.text: Next week you'll begin to look in more detail at developing your own personal brand.

chapters.title: Week 4: Developing my personal brand
chapters.summary: Identify your values, strengths, personality and career goals, and pull them together into your personal brand story.

blocks.text: Last week you learned more about what personal branding is, how a personal brand can be used in the workplace, and some celebrity case studies, both good and bad.
This week you'll concentrate on defining the various elements of your own brand, understanding what you want it to achieve and exploring the key attributes you want to promote to others.

blocks.title: Video 1 Introduction to Week 4
blocks.note: A short animated introduction with no spoken audio. You'll begin by considering the different elements your personal brand might include: what you have to offer and what is important to you - exploring your values, identifying your strengths and describing your personality traits. Next you'll consider your career goals and start to write your story, pulling all those elements together.

blocks.text: By the end of this week, you will be able to:

items: recognise the key elements of your personal brand
articulate your values, strengths and personality traits more clearly
describe your career goals.

blocks.title: Keep your answers
blocks.text: You'll refer back to this week's activity answers for the rest of the course, so save them as you go.

pages.title: Three stages of developing my brand

blocks.text: Before you can promote your personal brand to employers or others who might influence your future career, there are three broad stages to putting it together:

items: **Know what you have to offer and what is important to you** - take stock of your values, strengths, behaviours, etc.
**Know what you want** - have a vision for where you want to be career-wise at a point in the future, e.g. three years' time.
**Know what you are going to say** - be ready to share your personal brand clearly and succinctly at every appropriate opportunity.

blocks.alt: A man stands in front of a white wall, as if in a gallery, looking at drawn icons such as a lightbulb, a clock, a target and a handshake.
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Figuring it out

blocks.text: This might sound straightforward, but many people find identifying their strengths and values difficult, and it can take time to do properly. Having a clear idea of who you are and what you enjoy will help you decide what to do next - whether that means setting your sights on a specific career or recognising the right opportunities when they arise.

In Week 1 you started to think about what your brand is now and whether it needs changing. This week you delve deeper into what's important to you and what you'd like to share with the working world. The activities are designed to be useful whatever your experience, but some of you may feel the need for more support.

blocks.title: Getting support
blocks.text: Identifying your values and strengths is something a careers adviser is well qualified to help with (e.g. the Open University Careers and Employability team). Alternatively, a coach, mentor or even a friend can provide support and feedback as you process your thoughts.
Feedback is an important tool: when you've decided on your values, strengths, etc., find ways to test your analysis with family, friends or colleagues.
