blocks.title: Activity 1 Find a friend (about 5 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Receiving feedback is extremely valuable for the self-assessment you'll do this week. Before you start, list the people you know and trust who could offer feedback on the values, strengths and personality traits you come up with.
blocks.model: Don't aim to collect feedback from everyone on your list for all the exercises - this could feel overwhelming for everyone involved, including you! Some people may be better placed to offer feedback on your skills and strengths, while others might comment more usefully on the personality traits you've identified.
points: List several people you know and trust.
You don't need feedback from everyone on every exercise.
Some people suit feedback on skills and strengths.
Others suit feedback on your personality traits.

pages.title: Knowing what I have to offer: values

blocks.alt: A pair of upturned hands holding a small brown paper package tied with string and an unmarked label.
blocks.caption: Figure 2 What do you have to offer?

blocks.text: Many careers professionals begin a discussion about occupational choice by focusing on your values, as several studies have shown that values often align with occupational preferences.

For example, it has been found that individuals preferring, choosing or attaining business occupations were generally high on utilitarian orientation and material values; people choosing medical occupations, social work, and teaching appeared to be high in social values, in particular on altruism.

blocks.title: Values
blocks.text: 'The things that you believe are important in the way you live and work' (Mind Tools Content Team, n.d.).
The more closely you can align your values with the way you live and work, the more satisfied you are likely to be.
Gayle Johnson is a freelance copywriter and coach who has consciously built her business around her values.

blocks.title: Video 1 Gayle Johnson - Values
blocks.note: Gayle describes values as principles or guiding lights - the foundations of everything. If you're strong in what you believe in, you can turn your hand to anything. Through reflective exercises she found her values were connection and compassion, and built her business around them. Seeing other copywriters work very differently, she was daunted at first ('I'm not a slick hipster marketing type'), but pretending would have used all her energy and she wouldn't have been as good. Instead she was clear about what she stood for - tuning into your values is being kind to yourself, working with yourself, not against it. Her website states she works with values-driven people, which attracts clients she loves working with. Values are a 'breadcrumb trail through the woods' and anchor points: when mistakes happen you can come back to them, recentre and go again; they attract the right clients 'like magnets'.

pages.title: Gayle's advice on finding your values

blocks.title: Video 2 Gayle Johnson - Values Advice
blocks.note: Gayle made a list of values and used a process of elimination, and also thought about situations where she'd felt alive, 'on fire' and working at her best, then asked what values those moments meant. Knowing your values anchors you in your own work and stops you comparing yourself to others: one person's values might be growth, ambition and wealth; another's harmony and community - they could do the same work, but their 'vibe' and how they interpret it would be very different. Tuning into your values can help you avoid imposter syndrome when starting a business or new role, because you're doing it your way and no one can take that away. Mistakes still happen, but your values are something to come back to that give you strength to keep going.

blocks.q: According to Gayle, how can knowing your values help when you start a new role or business?
options: It guarantees you will never make mistakes
It helps you avoid imposter syndrome because you're doing it your way
It means you can copy successful competitors
It tells you which industry to work in
blocks.explain: Gayle says values anchor you and stop you comparing yourself to others, helping you avoid imposter syndrome. Mistakes still happen, but you can always come back to your values.

blocks.text: This is an exercise commonly used in values work. Gayle has used it herself and with clients.

blocks.title: Activity 2 Identifying my values - Step 1 (about 20 minutes in total)
blocks.prompt: Spend a few minutes thinking about times when you felt happiest, proudest, most fulfilled - or, as Gayle puts it, 'alive', 'on fire' and 'working at my best'. Include examples from both your home and work life. Note them down.
blocks.model: Your core values are already reflected in what you do and say when you're comfortable in your environment. Recalling peak moments - at home and at work - gives you the raw material for identifying the values behind them in the next step.
points: Describe at least one time you felt happiest or proudest.
Include examples from both home and work life.
Note what made you feel alive or at your best.

blocks.alt: A word cloud of values shaped like a speech bubble, with prominent words such as freedom, compassion, individuality, responsibility, equality, justice and humility.
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Which values will you choose?

blocks.title: Activity 2 Identifying my values - Step 2
blocks.prompt: Consider the values that best represent why those times made you feel so positive, and list them. Use the word cloud for ideas, add others that fit better, or search online for 'core values'. Go with your initial reaction to each word - don't overthink it.
blocks.model: Look for the values that explain why each peak moment felt good - for example freedom, compassion, individuality, responsibility or community. Trust your first reaction; you will narrow the list down in the next step.
points: List several values linked to your positive experiences.
Explain why each value made those times feel good.
Go with your initial reaction rather than overthinking.

blocks.title: Activity 2 Identifying my values - Step 3
blocks.prompt: Narrow down your list to between three and five core values and list them.
blocks.model: Your core values are already reflected in what you do and say, but labelling them helps make them more visible professionally and lets them influence your decision making; they should hold a prominent position in your personal branding. As Gayle explains, knowing them helps you feel comfortable about what you offer: several people may do the same job, but none with exactly your approach - that is what makes you unique. Values also help you recognise good opportunities: if you chose 'wealth', salary matters; if you value 'individuality', a workplace requiring conformity may be uncomfortable. Seek support if needed, e.g. from a careers adviser, coach or someone from your Activity 1 list.
points: Choose three to five core values.
Labelling values makes them more visible professionally and guides decisions.
Your values make your approach to work unique.
Values help you judge whether a role or workplace suits you.

blocks.text: Many of us don't deliberately think about our values, yet we all have them and they guide what we do. You might feel they're clearly expressed at home, but what about at work? Gayle talks about using values as **anchor points** to come back to - helpful when making career decisions.

Aligning your job with your values can be an important element of job satisfaction. If you strongly believe in accountability but colleagues seem to get away with mistakes and blaming others, that can make you angry, unhappy or demoralised. If you are self-employed and your values include freedom and independence, that should be a good match.
If you plan to use personal branding to find a more satisfying job, clearly communicating your values to your network and beyond is a good way to start.

pages.title: Knowing what I have to offer: strengths

blocks.text: A common explanation is that **strengths are innate**, whereas **skills can be learned and developed**. For example, your natural strength might be communication, but you've learned the skill of writing concise reports.

blocks.alt: A little girl dressed as a superhero in a red mask and cape raises her arm as if about to fly into the sky.
blocks.caption: Figure 4 What are my strengths?

blocks.text: In a career context, strengths are also thought of as the skills you most enjoy using; roles that let you use them are likely to bring satisfaction. Using your strengths energises you, whereas other activities can feel draining. Knowing your strengths won't necessarily lead to a new career path, but looking for opportunities to use them in new ways can make you happier (Seligman et al. 2005, p.416).

blocks.q: In the course's explanation, a skill is innate while a strength is something you learn.
blocks.explain: It is the other way round: strengths are innate, whereas skills can be learned and developed (e.g. a natural strength in communication, a learned skill of writing concise reports).

blocks.q: Which sign suggests you are using one of your strengths?
options: You were trained to do it
Your manager asked you to do it
blocks.explain: Using your strengths energises you, whereas other activities might feel draining.

blocks.title: Activity 3 Using my strengths (about 15 minutes)
blocks.prompt: 1) List the things you do, in work or outside, that really energise and enthuse you. 2) Choose one of those activities and analyse the skills you use when you do it - e.g. communicating with others, organising something, being creative. 3) Of those skills, which ones make you feel energised when you use them? Is it all of them or just certain ones? List them.
blocks.model: The skills you listed in the last step are your strengths. This is a quick exercise; if you found it useful, repeat it for all the activities you enjoy. Are there strengths that come up again and again? When you have a clear picture of your strengths you can add them to your personal brand.
points: List activities that energise you.
Break one activity down into the skills it uses.
The skills that energise you are your strengths.
Repeat for other activities to find recurring strengths.

blocks.text: If you struggled to define your strengths, many lists are available. Holloway (2017, p.39) gives a selection that is more nuanced than most, including:

items: telling engaging stories
extracting key points
creating order from chaos
never ever give up
never miss a deadline
create harmony in a team
researching new concepts
effortlessly funny
unfaltering focus
up to the minute knowledge
ultra-calm in a crisis
intuitive empathy
technologically savvy
nurturing a network
stress-testing ideas

blocks.title: Reflect
blocks.text: Do you have any strengths on that list that you could use in new ways in your current role(s)?

pages.title: Knowing what I have to offer: personality

blocks.text: Your personality, combined with your values, strengths, knowledge and experience, is what gives you your unique personal brand. No-one else will be able to offer the same combination of factors.

blocks.alt: About fifty overlapping passport photos of people of different ages, genders and ethnicities pinned as if on a notice board.
blocks.caption: Figure 5 Everyone is unique

blocks.text: In Week 2 you considered the relevance of a 'brand personality' and the human traits attributed to a product or organisation. Now consider which elements of your own personality you might incorporate into your brand.

blocks.title: Activity 4 Describing myself (about 10 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Imagine you're at an event where everyone is meeting for the first time and someone asks you to describe yourself. What would you say? Focus on your personality traits - for example humble, direct, charming, passionate, irritable or odd! (David Ball's 'Big Long List of Personality Traits' offers prompts.) Write one or two short paragraphs.
blocks.model: People respond to this in different ways and are often too modest or self-deprecating. Did you focus on positive aspects or highlight negatives? Positive aspects are the obvious ones to share in your brand, but you can learn from the negatives too: a characteristic you describe as 'shyness' could actually highlight your ability to observe, listen and analyse.
points: Describe several of your personality traits.
Avoid being too modest or self-deprecating.
Positive traits are the obvious ones to share.
Reframe 'negative' traits, e.g. shyness as the ability to observe, listen and analyse.

blocks.text: Setting key goals for your future career is an important part of personal branding. Once you know what you're aiming for, you can tailor your brand and how you promote it.

blocks.alt: A straight road heads towards distant mountains, with 'START' and an arrow painted on the tarmac.
blocks.caption: Figure 6 Know where to start

blocks.text: You don't need a detailed career plan. At an early stage your goals might be broad, for example:

items: working in a certain context, e.g. with animals
achieving a specific status, e.g. managing a team
being based in a different location, e.g. overseas.

blocks.text: At this stage, promoting your brand could mean talking to people in roles that interest you or contacting employers who might facilitate those goals. This tells you whether your brand aligns with what they look for (more on employers in Week 5).
Even with developed plans, many successful careers grow from opportunities that arise unexpectedly. The key is to be open to them, so relevant goals might be to:

items: investigate interesting opportunities seriously and with positivity - asking 'how could I make that work?' rather than assuming 'that wouldn't work for me'
follow the social media channels of interesting people and organisations
attend an event, e.g. a conference or job fair, related to an area of work that interests you.

blocks.text: Here, promoting your brand might involve networking (Week 7) or commenting on the social media posts of key individuals (Week 6).

blocks.title: Activity 5 Identifying my career goals (about 15 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Try to answer this in 30 seconds: what are your three most important career goals right now? Then take a few minutes to consider how realistic they are given current constraints such as location, financial needs or family commitments. Can you tweak them to fit what you need? Rewrite them if necessary.
blocks.model: Life coach Bennie Louw (n.d.) explains his 'Quick List method': when you only have 30 seconds to write your three most important goals, your answers will be as accurate as if you had 30 minutes or three hours - your subconscious goes into a kind of 'hyper-drive' and your most important goals pop out, often to your surprise. Your goals may be short, medium or long term, which affects how long they take to achieve. In Week 8 you'll revisit them and plan the actions needed.
points: Write three career goals quickly, within 30 seconds.
Check them against constraints such as location, money and family.
Tweak or rewrite them to be realistic.
Goals may be short, medium or long term.

blocks.title: Need more support?
blocks.text: This is only a brief overview of goal setting. Many people seek help from a careers adviser or coach; the career planning section of the OU's Careers and Employability website is a useful start.

The final stage in defining your personal brand is to bring it all together. It can be useful to think of it as a story: start with a more detailed narrative, which you can edit to meet your needs later.

blocks.alt: An old-fashioned typewriter with 'What's your story?' typed on a sheet of paper.
blocks.caption: Figure 7 Find your story

blocks.text: You might present your story in different ways to your target audience (Weeks 6 and 7), but the main task now is to pull together your key elements: **career goals, values, strengths, personality** and **knowledge/experience**.
If you're struggling to get started, here's an example:

items: **Career goals:** Within 5 years, I want to be a successful freelance writer with clients across a range of organisations. If I can use my writing to influence change and innovation, that would be the cherry on the cake.

**Values:** Concern for others, creativity and independence. I'd be supporting or developing people, as a leader or service provider, in an autonomous role where I set my own timetable and use creativity to solve problems. My ideal workplace celebrates innovation. I have strong family values, so work must fit around my children.

**Strengths:** 1) interacting with people, communicating authentically and effectively at all levels; 2) written communication - I love writing and editing copy that helps people be the best they can be.

**Personality:** Kind, thoughtful, empathetic and warm, with a good sense of humour; I use these to bring people together and motivate them. I'm curious and enjoy learning and sharing new facts or skills.
**Knowledge and experience:** Over 20 years in higher education, with significant knowledge of the student experience and a particular interest in careers and employability.

blocks.title: Activity 6 My story (about 30 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Using what you've learned about yourself this week, summarise the key points under each heading, thinking about how they relate to your future career ideas: 1) career goals, 2) values, 3) strengths, 4) personality, 5) knowledge/experience. When you're happy with it, share it with someone from your Activity 1 list for feedback - it's easier to hear constructive feedback from people you know, like and trust than from an employer you're keen to work for.
blocks.model: This won't necessarily be the final version; you might make changes after more feedback, but you've made a great start. Once you've collected feedback, this isn't something you need to present to others again - it is not your 'elevator pitch'. It is a narrative you can draw on when planning consistent messages about who you are and what you have to offer. Save it, as you'll refer back to your personal brand story later in the course.
points: Cover all five headings: goals, values, strengths, personality, knowledge/experience.
Link each element to your future career plans.
Share it with a trusted person for feedback.
It is a narrative to draw on, not your elevator pitch.
blocks.hint: Use the example story on the previous page as a model.

blocks.text: Want to go deeper? Many useful books are listed in the course's Further reading section.

pages.title: Try it: build your personal brand

blocks.title: Try it: personal brand builder
blocks.intro: Work through the four cornerstones step by step - values, strengths, personality and vision - then your target audience, positioning and why. The builder checks your brand for consistency and drafts a brand statement you can edit.

blocks.title: Match each element of a personal brand to its description

pairs.def: The things you believe are important in the way you live and work
Innate qualities; the skills you most enjoy using and that energise you
Abilities that can be learned and developed, such as writing concise reports
Traits such as humble, direct or passionate that you'd use to describe yourself
A vision of where you want to be career-wise, e.g. in three years' time
A narrative pulling all the elements together that you can draw on for consistent messages

blocks.text: This quiz counts towards your badge. It has 15 questions; aim for 50% or more.

blocks.q: What is the first of the three broad stages to putting your personal brand together?
options: Know what you are going to say
Know what you have to offer and what is important to you
blocks.explain: The three stages are: know what you have to offer and what is important to you; know what you want; know what you are going to say.

blocks.q: 'Know what you want' means:
options: Having a vision of where you want to be career-wise at a point in the future
Listing every job vacancy you might apply for
blocks.explain: Stage 2 is having a vision for where you want to be career-wise in the future, e.g. in three years' time.

blocks.q: The course suggests testing your list of values and strengths with family, friends or colleagues.
blocks.explain: Feedback is an important tool: find ways to test your analysis with people you know and trust.

blocks.q: How does Mind Tools define values?
options: The skills you most enjoy using
The things that you believe are important in the way you live and work
The traits others see in you
blocks.explain: Mind Tools defines values as 'the things that you believe are important in the way you live and work'.

blocks.q: According to Sverko et al. (2008), people choosing social work, medicine or teaching tended to score high on:
blocks.explain: Those choosing medical occupations, social work and teaching appeared high in social values, in particular altruism; business occupations were linked with utilitarian and material values.

blocks.q: Which two values did Gayle Johnson build her business around?
blocks.explain: Gayle found her values came down to things like connection and compassion and built her business around them.

blocks.q: In Activity 2, how many core values are you asked to narrow your list down to?
blocks.explain: Step 3 asks you to narrow your list to between three and five core values.

blocks.q: If one of your core values is 'individuality', which work environment might be uncomfortable for you?
options: One that requires you to conform
blocks.explain: The discussion notes that if you value individuality, a work environment that requires you to conform might not be comfortable.

blocks.q: What does the course say is a common difference between strengths and skills?
options: Strengths are learned; skills are innate
Strengths are innate; skills can be learned and developed
They mean exactly the same thing
Skills are only used at work
blocks.explain: Strengths are innate, whereas skills can be learned and developed.

blocks.q: According to Seligman et al. (2005), what has the potential to make you happier?
options: Looking for opportunities to use your strengths in new ways
blocks.explain: Knowing your strengths alone won't necessarily lead to a new path, but using them in new ways has the potential to make you happier.

blocks.q: In Activity 4, someone describes themselves as 'shy'. How might they reframe this for their brand?
options: As an ability to observe, listen and analyse
As a reason to avoid networking
blocks.explain: The discussion suggests 'shyness' could highlight your ability to observe, listen and analyse.

blocks.q: What gives you your unique personal brand?
options: Your personality combined with your values, strengths, knowledge and experience
blocks.explain: Your personality, combined with your values, strengths, knowledge and experience, is a combination no-one else can offer.

blocks.q: Which of these is a relevant goal for someone wanting to be open to unexpected opportunities? Select all that apply.
options: Investigate interesting opportunities seriously and with positivity
Follow the social media channels of interesting people and organisations
Attend an event such as a conference or job fair
blocks.explain: The course suggests asking 'how could I make that work?', following interesting people and organisations, and attending relevant events.

blocks.q: Why does the 'Quick List method' give you only 30 seconds to write your three main career goals?
options: Because answers written quickly are as accurate as those given hours of thought
Because goals should be short term
blocks.explain: Bennie Louw says that with only 30 seconds your answers are as accurate as with 30 minutes or three hours - your most important goals 'pop out'.

blocks.q: Your personal brand story from Activity 6 is the same as your elevator pitch.
blocks.explain: It is not your elevator pitch; it is a narrative you can draw on when planning consistent messages about who you are and what you offer.

blocks.text: By now you should be feeling more confident about the various elements of your personal brand. You might have considered some of them for the first time and need more support to finalise your story, or you might have used this week's activities to hone and finish it.
You should now be able to:

items: recognise the key elements of your personal brand
articulate your values, strengths and personality traits more clearly
describe your career goals.

cards.back: Know what you have to offer; know what you want; know what you are going to say.
The things you believe are important in the way you live and work (Mind Tools).
Strengths are innate and energise you; skills can be learned and developed.
Write your three most important career goals in 30 seconds (Louw).
Career goals, values, strengths, personality and knowledge/experience pulled together.

blocks.text: Next week you'll view things from the employer's perspective: what they look for in a personal brand now and in the future. You are now halfway through the course.

chapters.title: Week 5: Promoting my brand to employers
chapters.summary: Identify and research your target audience, learn what employers look for now and in future, and why you must maintain your personal brand.

blocks.text: Last week you identified and summarised the key elements of your own personal brand, starting to consider what you might present to employers. This week you shift to the **employer perspective**: what they want to know about you and your brand, and how that might change in the future.

blocks.title: Video 1 Introduction to Week 5
blocks.note: A short introduction to the week: who your target audience is, what employers are looking for now and in the future, and why you need to maintain your personal brand.

blocks.text: By the end of this week you will be able to:

items: identify your target audience
describe what employers are looking for
understand the importance of maintaining your personal brand.

pages.title: Who do I want to promote myself to?

blocks.text: In Week 2 you looked at the importance of correctly identifying your target audience. Now you're ready to have a go yourself.

blocks.alt: A smiling woman in red sunglasses shouts into a megaphone against a plain blue background
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Spread the word

blocks.text: Remember the two-stage process: **1. Identifying your audience** and **2. Researching your audience**.
blocks.title: Two stages

blocks.text: The career goals you want to achieve will probably fall into one of three broad categories, each with a potentially different target audience.

items: **Enhancing your current situation** - gaining new responsibilities or an internal promotion. Audience: peers and colleagues, senior managers, members of the HR team in your organisation, etc.

**Changing your emphasis** - doing the same job for a different employer, or using your skills in a different context within your current organisation. Audience: individuals in other departments or companies, representatives from a relevant professional body or recruitment consultancy, etc.

**Doing something new** - starting your career, or wanting a complete change and a new challenge. Initially your audience might include people already doing the role you aspire to: they can help you research the role, the main employers and what they look for.

blocks.text: When researching organisations or individuals, take a three-pronged approach:

items: **Online** - company websites and social media feeds give insight into what's going on in an organisation; you may spot key individuals who regularly post and share your views. Professional bodies, trade organisations and publications often have news pages that keep you up to date with an industry.
**On paper** - most printed material is also online, but internal newsletters or more obscure trade publications can provide useful insight.

**In person** - go to industry events such as conferences, breakfast meetings and networking evenings (find them by following employers or professional bodies on social media, or via student membership). You learn things that aren't on websites or in print, meet people who can help you, and raise your profile - making more direct questions about employment easier.

blocks.title: Match each description to the right term

pairs.def: Seeking new responsibilities or an internal promotion; audience includes senior managers and HR
Same job for a different employer, or your skills in a new context; audience includes professional bodies and recruitment consultancies
Starting out or making a complete change; audience includes people already doing the role you aspire to
Company websites, social media feeds and news pages of professional bodies
Internal newsletters and more obscure trade publications
Conferences, breakfast meetings and networking evenings

blocks.text: The first stage is to identify your target audience; the second is to research it. Allow about 5 minutes.

blocks.title: Activity 1 My audience
blocks.prompt: Think about the career goals you identified in Week 4. Who will help you achieve them - employers, colleagues, peers, etc.? List your target audiences. Then choose one of them, research them and their organisation further, and note your key findings.
blocks.model: Once you have a clearer idea of the groups you plan to target, you can start to consider exactly what you want from them, e.g. information, insight, a job, etc., and plan how you are going to share your personal brand with them in a way that encourages them to engage with you.
points: Lists specific target audiences linked to your career goals
Researches at least one target and their organisation
Identifies what you want from each audience (information, insight, a job)
Plans how to share your brand so they engage with you

blocks.text: Some of this research will start to tell you what future employers are looking for.

The job market is constantly changing, so keeping on top of the latest trends helps you promote yourself and stay a step ahead of competitors. Employers all want different things - depending on their culture, work and industry - but some issues are common to many.

blocks.alt: Two men and a woman in business suits stand on boxes using telescopes to look across a barren landscape
blocks.caption: Figure 2 Looking carefully

blocks.text: Strengths

Strengths have gained traction with employers in recent years. Using employees' strengths is a win-win: staff who use their strengths have greater job satisfaction and commitment, and organisations benefit from higher engagement. Having identified your strengths in Week 4, you can promote them - and when they align with an employer's priorities, you know you'll be a good fit.
TargetJobs (n.d.) explains another reason recruiters of new graduates are interested in strengths:

It is also argued that strengths-based interviews and assessments provide graduates from all socio-economic backgrounds with an equal opportunity to succeed. The answers to the questions don't require you to have multiple examples from extracurricular activities or internships - examples that might be easier for students from more advantaged backgrounds to obtain.
Typical strengths-based interview questions

items: What motivates you?
What would your perfect day look like?
How do you judge success?
If a colleague was struggling to make a complex decision, what would you do to help?
Given a choice, would you prefer to be giving a presentation or double-checking data?

blocks.text: Many reports look at the skills employers need - some sector specific, some generic. For example:

items: After a survey of 2000 business leaders, LinkedIn Learning (Petrone, 2018) named the top four soft skills they'd like employees to learn: **leadership, communication, collaboration and time management**. If any are your strengths, promote them clearly in your brand.

The CBI/Pearson Education and Skills Survey (2017, p. 13) reports that over a third of employers were dissatisfied with graduate recruits' **self-management skills and resilience**, and their lack of **business and customer awareness** and **international cultural awareness**. If these are strengths for you, highlight them.

blocks.q: Which of these was NOT among LinkedIn Learning's top four soft skills (Petrone, 2018)?
blocks.explain: The four were leadership, communication, collaboration and time management.

blocks.text: Using your strengths is a key part of greater job satisfaction, but your other skills - gained through previous learning and experience - also play a crucial role in daily working life.

Even if something doesn't fill you with energy and enthusiasm, that doesn't mean you can't be good at it. Choosing a role that lets you feel highly engaged for some of the time motivates you to deal with the less interesting stuff.

pages.title: Work style: a more flexible workplace

blocks.text: As the workplace becomes more flexible, the standard 9-5 day in the office is changing.

items: **Remote working** - with the explosion of digital communication, more organisations encourage staff to work remotely.

**The 'gig economy'** - workers are paid for the 'gigs' they do. More of us work for ourselves, and companies bring in freelancers alongside permanent staff for key projects. They benefit from your expertise without paying pension or annual leave; you gain variety and flexibility.
**Short-term contracts** - give the employer a chance to assess and be impressed by your skills, and can lead to longer-term employment if you want it.

blocks.text: If flexibility appeals to you, research employers' attitudes to it during your target audience research - some are more flexible than others.
Allow about 25 minutes. Find an organisation you'd be interested in working for and look at its website or social media pages.

blocks.title: Activity 2 Analyse an organisation
blocks.prompt: Analyse what the organisation looks for from its employees: What is its vision or mission? What are its values? Which skills/strengths does it prioritise when recruiting (check current job adverts and job descriptions for common themes)? What issues is it facing at the moment (social media feeds help)? Then compare with the personal brand story from Week 4, Activity 6 (your values, strengths and personality traits). Are there any parallels?
blocks.model: This is a good way to assess whether your brand aligns with that of the organisation. It will rarely be a perfect match, but if there are several similarities - for example they list your strengths as skills they are looking for, or you can see your values reflected in what they say - it could be worth adding them to your target audience list.
points: Identifies the organisation's vision/mission and values
Notes the skills or strengths it prioritises in recruitment
Mentions current issues the organisation faces
Compares these with your own values, strengths and traits
Decides whether to add it to your target audience list

blocks.text: When you know which sector or industry you want to work in, focus your attention there. Professional bodies and trade journals often commission relevant research - for example on sector skills shortages - that will inform your engagement with employers in those areas.
If you have a strength that fills a skills gap in your sector, highlighting it makes you an even more attractive candidate.
The job market is in constant flux, so you need to keep up with how things develop in the future.

pages.title: The future of the world of work

blocks.text: Looking for reassurance that robots won't take all our jobs, we increasingly encounter professional **'futurists'**: people from a range of professions, with experience in strategy and planning, who focus on future trends, forecasting and change.

blocks.alt: A row of white humanoid robots wearing headsets sit at computer screens in a futuristic room
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Is this the future?

blocks.title: Video 2 The future of work - adapting your skills and 'selves' to succeed
blocks.note: A short video by professional services company EY explaining 'The Future of Work' and the skills that will be needed. Adaptability is a key theme.

blocks.text: **Adaptability** is a key theme in this and many other pieces on the future of work. Kokemuller (n.d.) explains that 'companies need employees who are open to new ideas, flexible enough to work through challenging issues, and generally able to cope when things don't go as planned.'
Adaptable people can:

items: come up with alternative solutions when their first suggestion is rejected
cope when unexpected new projects are given to them
deal with changes to their role
remain calm and confident when facing a dilemma.

blocks.text: Allow about 10 minutes. Answer this typical application form question.
Unsure how to structure your answer? Use the **STAR** model: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Put the emphasis on the action you took.
blocks.title: STAR model
Activity 3 How adaptable am I?
blocks.prompt: Describe a situation when you had to change the way you worked because of changing circumstances. How did you adapt?
blocks.hint: Situation - Task - Action - Result; most of your answer should describe your actions.
blocks.model: Sample answer. Situation: my employer introduced a new IT system at very short notice, fundamentally changing my daily activities. Task: I had to train my team to work with it efficiently. Action: despite initial reservations I researched the system, talked to colleagues in my sector already using it, invited one to talk to the team, took a small group to see it working at their premises, and worked closely with the installation team. Result: despite a few hiccups it was installed on time and the team felt confident and enthusiastic about using it.
points: Describes a specific situation of changing circumstances
States the task or responsibility
Focuses on the actions you personally took to adapt
Gives a clear, positive result

blocks.text: Even if adaptability isn't one of your strengths, you can develop it - becoming more adaptable to change is largely about **mindset**. Boss (2014) talks about the importance of redefining your motivation:

For instance, if personal growth is a primary motivator then try to see adaptability through the lens of self-improvement; if relationships are a key driver for you, then think about how rich and meaningful your relations with others will be after you adapt. How you frame the problem through your mind's eye is what determines your reaction, so if you redefine how you see the problem then you can set yourself up for success. Being ready and willing to adapt is half the battle.
Many organisations have a strong interest in the future of work; the course's Further reading lists useful sources to keep up with it.

pages.title: What employers say about personal branding

blocks.text: Professional services company PwC takes personal branding seriously: it runs online courses and sessions for students.

blocks.title: Video 3 Aspire to lead: career advice - develop your own personal brand
blocks.note: A short PwC career-advice video on developing your own personal brand.

blocks.text: Employers won't always call it your 'personal brand', but they want a clear impression of you and your abilities quickly. If you stand out from everyone else they are assessing, they will be impressed. A clear, targeted brand shows you've considered their needs and how you can align with and support them - and they won't have to waste time trying to figure you out.
Employers regularly look at our social media presence. Jobvite's 2016 Recruiter Nation Report surveyed 1600 HR professionals about the platforms they use to evaluate candidates:
Your **digital footprint** is the information about you that exists because of your online activity. Consider it before raising your profile - next week covers how to tidy it.
Employers increasingly help existing employees develop their brand. Homayun (2016) shares eight tips for enhancing your brand at work - a supportive employer may help with some:

items: **Network over lunch** - invite a colleague and find out what they do
**Help others** - offer help, perhaps over coffee
**Write a thank you note** to someone you appreciate, e.g. an office assistant
**Start a book club** - industry-specific or general business books
**Ask intelligent questions** - do your homework before meetings
**Get involved in a new project** - contribute outside your normal hours
**Be charismatic** - think about your body language
**Be noticed for the right reasons** - don't be late to meetings or work on your laptop throughout

pages.title: Activity 4 Being noticed for the wrong reasons

blocks.text: Allow about 5 minutes.

blocks.title: Activity 4 Being noticed for the wrong reasons
blocks.prompt: Think about someone at work with a work-related habit that annoys or frustrates you - for example, constantly playing with their phone in meetings, or repeatedly bringing up one topic regardless of relevance. How does it affect your opinion of them? Do others share your frustration?
blocks.model: We have all had colleagues who are nice people and good at their jobs but become annoying in certain contexts. It doesn't mean we can't work productively with them, but it affects our opinion of them and our desire to work with them more than we have to. If they knew a habit was damaging their personal brand, maybe they would change it. Do you have any annoying habits that might affect how your brand is perceived?
points: Describes a specific annoying work habit
Explains how it affects your opinion of the person
Recognises that such habits damage a personal brand
Reflects on your own habits and how they are perceived

pages.title: When your personal brand goes wrong

blocks.alt: The words 'You're fired!' revealed through a tear in brown paper
blocks.caption: Figure 4 Bad news

blocks.text: Employers won't always fire you, but you can get into a lot of trouble for communicating the wrong messages as part of your personal brand.

blocks.title: Activity 5 What did Sally do wrong?
blocks.prompt: Sally tweeted: 'Hooray! I've been offered a job at Bob's Diner. Now to decide if the money is worth smelling of stale chip fat every day...' Explain why you think this message was a bad idea.
blocks.model: Sally shared a negative view about her new employer. This could be bad for Bob's business and shows a lack of commitment. Future employers checking her social media would wonder if she might say negative things about them too, reducing her chances of an interview. It is based on a real case: another employee saw the tweet and showed his boss, who immediately retracted the job offer.
points: The message is negative about her new employer
It could harm the business's reputation
It shows a lack of commitment
Future employers may fear she would criticise them too
It could cost her the job offer or interviews

blocks.text: The internet is full of people who used Twitter or Facebook the wrong way:

items: **Kevin's complaints** - an intern tired of menial jobs at a printing company tweeted that his job was 'boring' and was fired the next day.
**Susie's Instagram habit** - she posted a picture of her messy desk; an open document on it contained confidential company information. A disciplinary hearing followed.
**Jennifer's drinking** - a teacher in a strongly religious US state posted a photo appearing to drink straight from a wine bottle at a family barbecue. The headteacher asked her to resign.
**Martin's misdemeanour** - he phoned in sick, then posted a poolside party photo tagging a friend who was Facebook friends with his boss. He lost a day's pay and future sympathy.

blocks.text: Your personal brand isn't just a tool to get a job you love - you must maintain it and be aware of it all the time. Keep your messages consistent wherever your employer might see them.

blocks.q: What are the two stages of the process for targeting your audience?
options: Writing a CV and attending interviews
Identifying your audience and researching your audience
Choosing a sector and applying for jobs
blocks.explain: First identify who your target audience is, then research them and their organisation.

blocks.q: You want a complete career change. Who might initially be part of your target audience?
options: People already doing the role you aspire to
Members of your current HR team only
blocks.explain: For 'doing something new', people already in the role can help you research it, the main employers and what they look for.

blocks.q: Strengths-based interviews are argued to give graduates from all socio-economic backgrounds an equal opportunity to succeed.
blocks.explain: TargetJobs notes they don't rely on examples from extracurricular activities or internships, which advantaged students may find easier to obtain.

blocks.q: In Jobvite's 2016 survey, which platform did recruiters use most to evaluate candidates?
blocks.explain: LinkedIn (87%) was followed by Facebook (43%) and Twitter (22%).

blocks.q: Which of these is a sign of adaptability according to Kokemuller?
options: Remaining calm and confident when facing a dilemma
Keeping your role exactly the same
blocks.explain: Adaptable people find alternative solutions, cope with unexpected projects and role changes, and stay calm facing dilemmas.

blocks.q: In the STAR model, where should the emphasis of your answer be?
blocks.explain: Your emphasis should be on the action you took.

blocks.text: You should now have a clearer sense of your chosen target audience and an awareness of what employers are looking for - strengths, key skills and flexible work styles - and how the world of work may change. You have also considered employers' views about personal branding and how the wrong messages can backfire.
You should now be able to:

items: identify your target audience
describe what employers are looking for
understand the importance of maintaining your personal brand.

blocks.text: This week you started to explore your personal brand online; next week you'll look at that in more detail.

chapters.title: Week 6: Promoting my brand online
chapters.summary: Check and tidy your digital footprint, then promote your brand through LinkedIn, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, blogging and at work.

blocks.text: Last week you considered how the needs of employers, now and in the future, might affect your personal brand. This week you focus on promoting your brand online: social media and the platforms you could join if you haven't already, e.g. LinkedIn. Most commentators advise focusing on **one platform** to start with, as maintaining a profile across several networks takes a lot of time.

blocks.title: Video 1 Introduction to Week 6 (no spoken audio)
blocks.note: This week you'll investigate your current online brand and how to tidy up your digital footprint; promote your brand through popular social media platforms including LinkedIn and Facebook; explore raising the profile of your online brand at work; and look briefly at how an online profile can boost your business if you're self-employed.

blocks.text: By the end of this week you will be able to:

items: identify any issues with your current online brand
recognise how to promote your brand online
describe how you might use various social media platforms to promote your brand.

pages.title: What is my current online brand?

blocks.text: A useful place to start is to assess what is currently out there. For example, you may have images on your Facebook page that are less than professional! Would you want a potential employer or professional contact to see them?

blocks.alt: A smartphone on a blue wooden surface showing a Social Media folder of app icons including Facebook, Snapchat and Instagram
blocks.caption: Figure 1 My online brand

blocks.text: If you want to step back and build your skills and confidence about life online first, the OpenLearn course *Digital literacy: succeeding in a digital world* is a great starting point.
Allow about 10 minutes. Googling you is what an employer or networking contact will often do.

blocks.title: Activity 1 Google it!
blocks.prompt: Enter your name into a search engine and see what comes up. Make sure you also check 'Images', where photos might appear. Note anything that surprises you, or that you want to delete or make private.
blocks.model: Did you find anything that surprised you? Sometimes we can be tagged in other people's photos unexpectedly. If unwanted content did come up, it might be a good idea to try other search engines too, e.g. Bing.
points: Searches your own name, including image results
Notes anything surprising or unwanted
Identifies content to delete or make private
Considers tags in other people's photos and other search engines

blocks.text: When you post something on a social media platform you are actually **publishing** it - and it can't always be retracted.
Grothaus (2018) offers these tips for tidying your digital footprint:

items: **Make your social media accounts private**
**Review your timelines** - remove photos or comments that could cast you in a negative light
**Control tagging** - tags with your name can appear in Google searches. Untag yourself, ask friends to untag you, or find out how to stop others tagging you
**Find and close old accounts** - Google your name or try a service like Deseat.me, which aims to find your forgotten online accounts.

blocks.text: If you can't delete everything, Majeed (2016) suggests frequently posting more positive material to drive out negative results, and using **Google Alerts** to tell you whenever you are mentioned online.

pages.title: Ten top tips for your digital footprint

blocks.title: Video 2 Ten top tips to improve your digital footprint
blocks.note: From the OpenLearn course Digital Literacy: Succeeding in a Digital World. Delete or deactivate accounts you no longer use (tools online can help). For accounts you keep, filter out people you don't know or no longer keep in touch with - Facebook tends to be personal, while LinkedIn needs a professional network and more public settings if you want to be noticed. Delete unflattering photos and posts you're not proud of. Build your LinkedIn profile like an online CV with achievements, skills, qualifications and knowledge, using the words employers might search for. Be active on Twitter with professional content; start or comment on professional blogs; join discussion forums to learn and share good practice.

blocks.q: The video advises using the words employers might search for when writing your LinkedIn profile.
blocks.explain: Employers and agencies frequently search LinkedIn for specific skills, so think about the words they would search for.

blocks.text: Once you've cleaned up your existing brand, you can start promoting your new one.
Think back to your personal brand story from Week 4, Activity 6, and keep that content in mind throughout this week. If you downloaded or printed your activity answers, refer to them.

pages.title: Using LinkedIn to promote my brand

blocks.text: LinkedIn is a social networking platform for professionals, with more than 562 million users in over 200 countries and territories. Its stated vision is to 'Create economic opportunity for every member of the global workforce.'

blocks.alt: A laptop on a table showing the LinkedIn sign-up page: 'Join the world's largest professional network'
blocks.caption: Figure 2 Using LinkedIn

blocks.text: Social media isn't for everyone, but of all the platforms discussed this week, LinkedIn is the one professionals should seriously consider engaging with.
Nations (2018) recommends these uses for beginners:

items: Get back in touch with old colleagues
Use your profile as your CV or resume
Find and apply for jobs
Find and connect with new professionals
Participate in relevant groups
Blog about what you know.

blocks.text: One of the most valuable ways to build your brand on LinkedIn is to **join relevant groups and contribute regularly** to their conversations. LinkedIn Help (n.d.): 'You can find groups to join by using the search feature at the top of your homepage or viewing groups you've already joined. You can also create a new group focused on a specific topic or industry.'

Allow about 10 minutes. The **summary section** appears at the top of your profile and is the first thing people read. It's usually no more than two or three paragraphs - a chance to grab attention and encourage people to read on. Treat it like a personal profile on a CV. If you have a profile, update your summary; if not, consider setting one up.

blocks.title: Activity 2 My LinkedIn profile
blocks.prompt: Using your personal brand story for ideas, compose your LinkedIn summary (two or three paragraphs).
blocks.hint: Try one of Frost's templates: mission-based, personality, short and sweet, blended or accomplishments.
blocks.model: Frost (n.d.) suggests templates: the mission-based summary (broad description of what you do, then more specific); the personality summary (opens with an anecdote showing one or two key traits); the short and sweet summary (current role, previous positions and skills - good for technical or conservative industries); the blended summary (personality plus mission, light, fun and professional); and the accomplishments summary (why you deserve the job).
points: Two or three short paragraphs that grab attention
Draws on your values, strengths and brand story
Reads like a personal profile on a CV
Follows a clear structure, e.g. one of Frost's templates

blocks.title: Match each description to the summary style (Frost, n.d.)

pairs.def: Opens with a broad description of what you do, then gets more and more specific
Begins with an anecdote that demonstrates one or two key personality traits
Shares current role, previous positions and skills; useful for technical or conservative industries
Combines personality and mission to create something light, fun and professional
Tells potential employers why you deserve the job

pages.title: Using Facebook to promote my brand

blocks.text: Facebook is a social networking website and service where users can post comments, share photographs and links to news or other content, play games, chat live and stream live video (Nations, 2018). It has over 2 billion active users and, after LinkedIn, is the second most likely platform recruiters use to evaluate your brand.

blocks.alt: A hand holds a smartphone showing the Facebook log-in page, with a laptop in the background
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Using Facebook

blocks.text: Facebook traditionally connects family and friends, but professionals increasingly use it to promote what they do - building communities of like-minded people to share content with and advertise services to. Like LinkedIn, it offers lots of groups to join and contribute to, and you could even start one yourself.
The key to success on any platform is to post comments, ideas and content **regularly**. This is time-consuming and can slip when life is busy - so make sure you have time to commit.

Caution: remember Week 5 on the negative impact of saying the wrong things. If you voice opinions on controversial subjects such as politics or religion, think carefully about whether they align with the brand you want to promote.
blocks.title: Caution

pages.title: Activity 3 What could I post about?

blocks.text: Allow about 20 minutes. Even if you won't use Facebook, generating post ideas is useful - they can also feed blogs or workplace discussions. For example, with knitting as a theme you could: suggest designs for a coming special day (Mother's Day, Christmas); offer advice on a tricky technique; say what you most enjoy about it; or address an issue other knitters feel strongly about.

blocks.title: Activity 3 What could I post about?
blocks.prompt: 1. Pick a theme you know about, enjoy or feel strongly about (work-related or a hobby). 2. List as many different ways as you can to talk about that theme - keep going until you run out of ideas. 3. Look back through your ideas and list any connections with your personal brand, e.g. your values, strengths or experience.
blocks.model: You might not want to post about your hobbies, but sharing something about yourself gives others a sense of what you stand for and have to offer. Sharing views can be daunting given possible negative feedback, so choosing the right groups and finding the right, 'authentic' voice is important. What you share needn't be personal: you can curate content from other experts or organisations so others are informed and inspired without searching for it themselves.
points: Chooses a clear theme
Generates several varied post ideas
Links ideas to your values, strengths or experience
Considers an authentic voice and the right groups
Recognises curating others' content as an option

blocks.alt: Seven people sitting in a row on a bench, seen from the neck down, each using a tablet, laptop or phone
blocks.caption: Figure 4 Lots of ways to get online

blocks.text: **Twitter** is an online news and social networking site where people communicate in short messages called tweets (280 characters or less). It has 330 million active users. Gil (2018): most tweet recreationally, but a growing number send really useful content - 'a stream of quick updates from friends, family, scholars, news journalists, and experts.'

For your brand, share news and views, follow others in your industry and 'retweet' their messages with your own comments. Etiquette suggests you follow people who follow you (unless you're a public figure), which helps you get noticed by key people. Tweet regularly to maintain your profile.
**Instagram** is a social networking app for sharing photos and videos, with 800 million users.

Professionally, sharing images works well if you are in a creative industry or have a visual brand to promote, and it lets you show what you do visually. The most popular users often mix personal and professional life - pictures of their working day alongside holiday shots or cakes they've made.
Think again about your personal brand story: can you encapsulate it visually? Would that be a useful approach?

blocks.title: Video 3 What is a blog?
blocks.note: A short video explaining what blogging is.

blocks.text: Blogging professionally, Johnson (2018) suggests four reasons to blog:

items: To increase your audience - invite them to connect
To connect more deeply with prospective clients - sharing the real you
To position yourself as an expert - show what you know
To reach more people with your message - invite guest bloggers and you'll reach their audience too.

blocks.text: Make sure your blog reaches your target audience: link to posts in email, on LinkedIn, Facebook, Twitter, etc., or invite people you admire to write guest posts.

blocks.title: Match each description to the platform

pairs.def: Professional network whose vision is to 'create economic opportunity for every member of the global workforce'
Over 2 billion users; traditionally for family and friends, the second platform recruiters check
Short messages of 280 characters or less; retweet others' messages and add your comments
Photo and video sharing; works well for creative industries or a visual brand
Position yourself as an expert and reach more people through guest posts

blocks.text: Allow about 20 minutes. Review the platforms discussed this week - LinkedIn, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram and blogging. Consider how others use them professionally and ask colleagues, friends or family what they use and why.

blocks.title: Activity 4 Choose a platform
blocks.prompt: Choose the one platform you are most likely to use to promote your personal brand, and note your reasons.
blocks.model: Depending on your circumstances, you may decide that promoting your personal brand online is not a priority now. But as the digital world continues to grow and extend its influence over our professional lives, you may need to reconsider in the future.
points: Names one platform to focus on
Gives reasons linked to your goals and target audience
Draws on how others use it professionally
Recognises that priorities may change as the digital world grows

pages.title: Raising your online profile at work

blocks.alt: The words 'Boost your brand' spelled out in old wooden printing blocks beside a mug of coffee
blocks.caption: Figure 5 Boosting your brand

blocks.text: At work your brand is often communicated face to face (Week 7 covers this), but an online profile with colleagues can share elements of your brand they might not see day to day.

Starting a **blog** on topics close to you and your colleagues' hearts raises your profile and lets you share your views differently. If colleagues already blog, or write for a departmental blog, you could share post ideas, offer to guest blog or simply comment - building your voice without running a blog yourself.

pages.title: Newsletters, emails and LinkedIn at work

items: **Online newsletter** - offer to write short articles for your department's newsletter.
**Email** - a thought-provoking email to key people suggesting improvements to a project or asking key questions shows you are committed and engaged.
**LinkedIn** - connecting with colleagues gives access to their connections, some of whom may be interesting contacts.

blocks.text: When inviting people you don't know, it's better to ask a mutual connection to introduce you - people are more likely to accept via someone they know. Once connected, comment on their posts or message them to introduce yourself.
Likewise, don't accept every invitation: some people just want access to your contacts, and your network is more useful if connections are relevant and add value.

blocks.q: To build a useful LinkedIn network you should accept invitations from everyone who invites you.
blocks.explain: Some may just want access to your contact list; relevant connections that add value make your network more useful.

blocks.text: If you're self-employed, raising your profile online has a double advantage: people understand your personal brand, and you can leverage that awareness to sell products or services. Once you have an engaged audience, devise your **'call to action'** - inviting them to buy your products or expertise.

blocks.title: Video 4 Gayle Johnson - Profile
blocks.note: Copywriter Gayle Johnson (Red Tree Writing) chose to do one platform well - Facebook - rather than spread herself thinly. Setting up her page felt daunting and at first little happened. She uses it to start conversations and build relationships, sharing snippets of her work, behind the scenes and clients' good news, with only occasional offers. Letting people into her world builds trust. Even more powerful is her active Facebook group: members share tips and questions about writing and build friendships, and it is where most of her business comes from - when people need a writer she's the first person who comes to mind, and evidence of client successes builds trust.

blocks.text: Allow about 10 minutes. Although Gayle speaks from a small business perspective, what she says about relationship building applies in many contexts.

blocks.title: Activity 5 Engaging your target audience
blocks.prompt: Consider the platform you chose in Activity 4. What can you take from Gayle's experience to develop your approach? Who might you want to build a relationship with to enhance your career?
blocks.model: Rather than using social media simply to sell what you have to offer, Gayle talks about starting a conversation and building relationships. These connections can grow into opportunities or provide evidence of your commitment to, or knowledge and expertise in, a particular subject.
points: Applies Gayle's ideas to your chosen platform
Focuses on conversation and relationships rather than selling
Names specific people or groups to build relationships with
Sees connections as a route to opportunities and evidence of expertise

blocks.title: Video 5 Gayle Johnson - Profile Advice
blocks.note: Choose one or two platforms and do a few things well rather than juggle many. Let people into your world - it can be curated: your audience only needs the bits that help them connect with you, and that is still authentic. Be human online and don't use it purely as a selling machine; sales happen organically. Don't be afraid to share opinions and expertise - share tips, ask questions and invite interaction, because social media works best as a conversation, not a stream of adverts.

cards.back: The information about you that exists because of your online activity
Inviting an engaged audience to buy your products or expertise
Pulling together and posting other experts' or organisations' content so others are informed without searching
A tool that tells you whenever you are mentioned online
Writing posts for someone else's blog, or inviting others to write for yours, to reach a wider audience

blocks.q: Why do most commentators advise focusing on one social media platform to start with?
options: Maintaining profiles across several networks takes a lot of time
blocks.explain: Maintaining several profiles is time-consuming; Gayle Johnson likewise recommends doing one or two well.

blocks.q: Which of these is one of Grothaus's (2018) tips for tidying your digital footprint?
options: Find and close old social media accounts
blocks.explain: Grothaus suggests making accounts private, reviewing timelines, controlling tagging and closing old accounts.

blocks.q: If you can't delete negative content about you, Majeed suggests posting positive material frequently to drive it out of search results.
blocks.explain: Frequent positive posts push negative results down; Google Alerts can tell you when you are mentioned.

blocks.q: When inviting someone you don't know to connect on LinkedIn, what is the best approach?
options: Ask a mutual connection to make an introduction
Message them only about job vacancies
Wait for them to find you
blocks.explain: People are more likely to accept an invitation that comes via someone they know.

blocks.q: Which is one of Johnson's (2018) four reasons to blog professionally?
options: To position yourself as an expert
blocks.explain: The four reasons: increase your audience, connect more deeply with prospective clients, position yourself as an expert, reach more people with your message.

blocks.q: According to Gayle Johnson, where does most of her business come from?
blocks.explain: Her group built a community; when people need a writer she is the first person who comes to mind.

blocks.text: You now have a greater awareness of ways to boost your personal brand online - checking and tidying your digital footprint, then using LinkedIn, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram or blogging - and how to use these tools to raise your profile in your current workplace or your own business.
You should now be able to:

items: identify any issues with your current online brand
recognise how to promote your brand online
describe how you might use various social media platforms to promote your brand.

blocks.text: Next week you'll look at promoting your personal brand in person and on paper.

chapters.title: Week 7: Promoting my brand in writing and in person
chapters.summary: Convey your personal brand in job applications, CVs, emails, reports and business cards, and in person through first impressions, networking and interviews.

blocks.text: Last week you focused on promoting your brand online, via popular social media platforms including LinkedIn and Facebook.
This week, you'll explore how to promote your brand **in writing and in person**. These interactions occur all the time in the workplace, and you'll learn how to be ready to respond when they do.

blocks.title: Video 1 Introduction to Week 7
blocks.note: A short video that introduces this week's theme: promoting your personal brand in writing and in person.

blocks.text: By the end of this week, you will be able to:

items: emphasise your personal brand during the job application process
demonstrate your personal brand in day-to-day interactions
recognise opportunities to promote your personal brand in writing and in person.

blocks.text: The emphasis here is on how to convey your personal brand effectively in your applications, not on the actual process of filling them in. Many online resources can help with application forms and CVs - for example, the Open University Careers and Employability pages on CVs, application forms and interviews.
blocks.title: Study note

blocks.text: Most application forms require some form of **personal statement**, outlining how you meet the requirements for the job. The usual process is to go through the job description and person specification for the role and ensure that you address their key requirements as you write your statement.

If you find it difficult to focus on your personal brand as you write, start by responding to the role requirements first - detailing your relevant experience, etc. as you normally would. After the first draft, read it through to check for the prominence of your personal brand and look for opportunities to reinforce it throughout.

pages.title: Weaving your brand into a statement

blocks.text: For example, the job requires attention to detail and you also want to emphasise your person-centred values. Rather than simply stating that you have good attention to detail and giving some evidence, you might say instead:

I pay close attention to detail because I want to ensure that individuals can engage with the service I provide as quickly and easily as possible. They can then focus their attention on the things that are important to them and their work. For example, I recently produced a well-received user manual for our email system.

Thus, you have emphasised your personal strength - **concern for others**. You've explained the **benefit to the employer** (saving colleagues' time), and given an **example** they can explore further in your interview.
The aim is to make yourself stand out from other candidates enough to be invited for interview.

blocks.alt: A hand holding a pen, poised to begin filling out an application form
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Filling out an application form

blocks.text: Competency-based questions

Some application forms ask a series of competency-based questions focusing on the key skills the organisation is looking for. In Week 5, Activity 3, you answered a question about adaptability - a typical example. The format differs from a personal statement, but the same principle applies: make sure your personal brand is reflected in each answer.
Strengths-based questions

These focus on what you *enjoy* doing rather than what you *can* do, e.g. 'Describe an occasion when you achieved something you were really proud of'. This is a perfect opportunity to share your brand. Use the strengths you identified in Week 4, and keep in mind the strengths the employer is looking for, so your answer is as relevant to them as possible.
Check that you can tell the two types of application question apart.

blocks.q: 'Describe an occasion when you achieved something you were really proud of.' What type of application question is this?
blocks.explain: Strengths-based questions focus on what you enjoy doing rather than what you can do - a perfect opportunity to share your personal brand.

blocks.q: With competency-based questions the format is different from a personal statement, so you no longer need to reflect your personal brand in your answers.
blocks.explain: The format is slightly different, but the same principle applies: try to ensure your personal brand is reflected in each answer.

blocks.text: The **personal profile** or personal objective, which comes at the top of your CV, can easily be adapted to incorporate your personal brand. It should give the employer a clear introduction to your CV, grabbing their attention and encouraging them to read on.
The mistake many people make with their personal profile is to write something **vague and generic**. It needs to be:

items: unique to you
backed up by some concrete facts
consistent with the content of the rest of your CV.

pages.title: Activity 1 A personal profile for my CV

blocks.title: Activity 1 A personal profile for my CV (about 10 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Here is a typical personal profile: 'I'm a dedicated team player with retail experience. I have successfully managed a small concession in a large department store and have demonstrated my ability to make a profit. I am an excellent motivator and can work effectively with a wide range of customers and colleagues.' How could personal brand be made clearer in that profile? What facts could be included? Write your suggestions.
blocks.model: A stronger version combines personal brand with concrete facts: 'I have three years of retail experience, mainly in women's clothing. In my current Concession Manager role, I enjoy using my creativity and strong communication skills to inspire both colleagues and customers with my ideas and suggestions. This has resulted in a 20% profit increase in only four months.' An employer would see evidence for the communication claim, an early-career record of increasing profits, someone who knows their strengths and cares about colleagues and customers, and would want to read on about the Concession Manager role.
points: Replace vague, generic claims with concrete facts and figures (e.g. years of experience, profit increase).
Provide evidence for claims such as being a good communicator or motivator.
Show your strengths and values (e.g. creativity, caring about colleagues and customers).
Make the employer want to read further down the CV.
blocks.hint: Think about numbers, the specific role, what you enjoy and what result you achieved.

blocks.text: Your personal brand can be reflected throughout your CV. For example, you can highlight key strengths throughout your employment history and perhaps demonstrate your values by discussing your voluntary work.

The key to writing an effective CV is **tailoring it to each employer** you send it to. Aligning your personal brand with their company values, or the strengths you know they look for in their employees, should put you ahead of much of your competition.
Support this approach with evidence that demonstrates when you have used these values and strengths - then you'll be ticking a lot of the employers' boxes.

The most difficult thing to get across effectively in an email is **tone**. How many times have you read an email and felt slightly disgruntled by the sender's attitude - when they might not have intended to come across like that? Staying true to your personal brand might help you to avoid that situation yourself.
Holloway (2017) recommends that you start your emails with something that will **build rapport**, for example:
Hope all's well in the accounts department on this horrible rainy day. I'm not looking forward to cycling home!
Thanks for your message last week, I'm sorry it's taken me so long to reply - a series of small crises has kept me away from email for a few days.
This gives the recipient an opportunity to refer to your comment in their reply ('I got wet on my way home too!'), which starts to build rapport between you.

blocks.alt: A woman sits on the floor with her laptop open, surrounded by colourful cartoon envelopes hovering in the air
blocks.caption: Figure 2 You've got mail

blocks.text: There are various ways to communicate your personal brand via email:

items: By being authentic in your tone and language
By drawing attention to shared experience or shared values
By asking the recipient if they have time for a coffee to discuss the issue - which also gives you a chance to demonstrate your brand in person

By always responding quickly and efficiently, e.g. sending a holding email if a full reply will take time. The recipient is more likely to pay attention to your tone and content if they are not furious about how long you took to reply!

blocks.text: Meetings inevitably involve paperwork, and sometimes you might be the author - of a report or update on a project, a bid for funding, or a proposal to change something. Your readers will form opinions about you based on what they read.
Even if the topic is unrelated to your personal brand, you can get consistent messages about your brand across. Consider what you want the reader to think about you as they read it, e.g.:

items: He really knows what he's talking about
Some serious research has gone into this document
She seems to have consulted widely
He cares about the people this will impact on
She isn't afraid of change
He has some creative ideas
Her team are clearly behind her.

blocks.text: Some commentators predicted that social media would kill off the business card, but it hasn't happened yet. For many it remains a useful tool because:

items: it stops you from getting lost in someone's phone contact list
it serves as a useful reminder of your brand whenever someone comes across it in their wallet, bag or desk drawer
you don't have to waste time spelling out your email address as they type it into their phone - just exchange cards and follow up later.

blocks.text: Many of us are restricted by our organisation's card design, but if you could design your own, how would you convey your personal brand? Think back to Week 3, Activity 3, when you thought about what **colour** your brand would be - this could be the time to use it.

If you can encapsulate your personal brand in a statement, that could also be included on your card. BrandYourself (2017) describes the following examples as your 'catchphrase' about your specific experience:

items: I help people create new opportunities in their businesses and careers
I am a personal trainer, specialising in weight training and mobility
I give authors visibility on untapped promotional platforms where they can share their work
I spark new product ideas for large companies that have stagnant product cycles.

blocks.text: Although these don't include a job role or title, you can see how a **focus on what you can do for others** might strengthen your offering.

blocks.title: Activity 2 My personal brand statement (about 10 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Try to encapsulate your personal brand in a single sentence suitable for a business card. Write it below.
blocks.model: Even if you don't plan to produce your own business cards, being able to summarise your brand in a sentence is a useful opener to discussions about what you do and why someone should be interested. It might become the first line of your elevator pitch, which you'll look at in more detail in Week 8.
points: Summarise your personal brand in one short sentence.
Focus on what you can do for others rather than just a job title.
Reflect your specific experience, strengths or values.
It could become the first line of your elevator pitch.
blocks.hint: Try the pattern 'I help ... to ...' or 'I ... for people who ...'.

blocks.text: There are many contexts in which face-to-face interaction will allow you to promote your personal brand.
First impressions count - and they are formed even before we start to speak.

blocks.title: Video 2 Jayne Chapman - First Impressions
blocks.note: Business Image Specialist Jayne Chapman explains that first impressions are made within a few seconds (some researchers say milliseconds). A positive first impression puts you 'one step forward' in a relationship before you've opened your mouth and helps people receive what you have to say; a negative one puts you a step back.
